# Vision: Classification

Classify and describe an image (requires vision model)

<!-- TODO review -->
Sort images into categories, tag them for search, or describe them for people who cannot see
them. It needs a vision-capable model, so on this site it prints a message instead of running;
run it locally with the batteries, as in [Vision: OCR](/vision-ocr/).

```ajs:inline
function classifyImage({ imageUrl = '/photo-1.jpg' }) {
  // Fetch image as data URL
  let image = httpFetch({ url: imageUrl, responseType: 'dataUrl' })

  // Schema for classification result
  let schema = Schema.response('image_classification', {
    category: '',
    subject: '',
    description: '',
    tags: [''],
    confidence: '',
  })

  let result = llmVision({
    prompt:
      'Classify this image. Identify the main subject, provide a brief description, and list relevant tags.',
    images: [image],
    responseFormat: schema,
  })

  let parsed = JSON.parse(result.content)
  return { imageUrl, classification: parsed }
}
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

- **Free-form categories drift.** With `category: ''` the model invents a new word for the same
  thing from one image to the next. If you will group or filter on it, close the set (variation
  below).
- **`confidence` is the model's own opinion of itself**, as text. Treat it as a hint, not a
  probability.
- **The same shape as OCR.** Fetch as a data URL, ask `llmVision` with a schema, parse
  `result.content`. Only the prompt and the schema change.

<!-- TODO review -->
## A variation

A fixed set of categories, with `Schema.enum`, and a yes/no question the program can act on:

```javascript
function screenImage({ imageUrl = 'https://images.example.com/upload.jpg' }) {
  let image = httpFetch({ url: imageUrl, responseType: 'dataUrl' })
  let schema = Schema.response(
    'screening',
    Schema.object({
      category: Schema.enum(['person', 'animal', 'landscape', 'document', 'other']),
      containsText: Schema.boolean,
      altText: Schema.string,
    })
  )
  let result = llmVision({
    prompt: 'Categorize this image and write one sentence of alt text for it.',
    images: [image],
    responseFormat: schema,
  })
  let screening = JSON.parse(result.content)
  return { imageUrl, screening, needsOcr: screening.containsText }
}
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## The gotcha

The image a model sees is the image the agent fetched, so the same trust rules apply as to text:
an image can contain written instructions, and a model may follow them. Decide what happens next
in code (`needsOcr` above), not by asking the model what to do.

It needs a vision-capable model, so on this site it prints a message instead of running; run it locally with the batteries, as in [Vision: OCR](/vision-ocr/).

# LLM Code Solver

LLM writes and runs code to solve a problem (requires llm capability)

<!-- TODO review -->
An agent that writes a program and runs it. Models reason badly about loops and numbers but
write small programs well, so for a question like "the 10th Fibonacci number" it is more
reliable to ask for code and run it than to ask for the answer. That is only reasonable because
the code runs in the same sandbox as the agent. It needs an LLM, so on this site it prints a
message instead of running; run it locally with the host from [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/), plus the
`code` capability described below.

````ajs:inline
function solveWithCode({ problem = 'Calculate the 10th Fibonacci number' }) {
  // System prompt with AsyncJS rules and example
  let systemContext =
    'You write AsyncJS code. AsyncJS is a JavaScript subset.\n\nRULES:\n- Functions take a destructured object param: function foo({ a, b })\n- MUST return an object. WRONG: return 42. RIGHT: return { result: 42 }\n- NO: async, await, new, class, this, var, for loops\n- Use let for variables, while for loops\n\nEXAMPLE (factorial):\nfunction solve() {\n  let result = 1\n  let i = 5\n  while (i > 1) {\n    result = result * i\n    i = i - 1\n  }\n  return { result }\n}\n\nReturn ONLY the function code, nothing else.'

  let prompt =
    systemContext + '\n\nWrite a function called "solve" that: ' + problem

  let response = llmPredict({ prompt })

  // Clean up code - remove markdown fences, fix escapes, extract function
  let code = response
  code = code.replace(/```(?:javascript|js|asyncjs)?\n?/g, '')
  code = code.replace(/\n?```/g, '')
  code = code.replace(/\\n/g, '\n')
  code = code.replace(/\\t/g, '\t')
  code = code.replace(/\\"/g, '"')
  code = code.trim()

  // Try to extract just the function if there's extra text
  let funcMatch = code.match(/function\s+solve\s*\([^)]*\)\s*\{[\s\S]*\}/)
  if (funcMatch) {
    code = funcMatch[0]
  }

  // Validate it looks like a function before running
  if (!code.startsWith('function')) {
    return {
      problem,
      error: 'LLM did not generate valid code',
      rawResponse: response,
    }
  }

  // Execute the generated code
  let output = runCode({ code, args: {} })

  return {
    problem,
    generatedCode: code,
    result: output.result,
  }
}
````

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

- **The fence has four backticks** because the code contains three (it strips Markdown fences
  from the model's answer). Models wrap code in fences however firmly you ask them not to.
- **Cleanup is ordinary string work.** The `replace` and `match` calls run on the VM's own regex
  engine and are metered like everything else.
- **`runCode({ code, args })` transpiles and runs the generated source** as its own program: a
  fresh scope that sees only `args`, never the caller's variables or helpers. It shares the
  caller's fuel, heap budget, capabilities and quotas, so generated code can do nothing the agent
  could not already do.
- **It needs the `code` capability.** Running code is a privilege the host grants, like the
  network: without `code.transpile` the call fails with `Capability 'code.transpile' missing`.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Running it locally

Add a `code` capability to the host from [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/). Transpiling runs on the host,
before any fuel is charged, so the VM caps the size of the source first:

```javascript
const vm = new AgentVM()
const code = { transpile: (source) => transpile(source, { atoms: vm.atoms }).ast }
await vm.run(ast, {}, { fuel: 2000, capabilities: { llm, code } })
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## The gotchas

- **Generated code fails like any code.** A program that does not transpile is an error the
  agent can catch (`Code transpilation failed: …`); one that loops forever runs out of fuel,
  taking the agent's budget with it. Give the run a budget sized for both.
- **Generated code can call `runCode` too**, so nesting is capped at 10 levels.
- **The prompt matters more than the cleanup.** The system text above is a short version of
  [the maintained AJS prompt](/ajs-llm-prompt/), which is tuned (and measured) for small models.
  Note that it still forbids `for` loops entirely; AJS has `for...of`, only the C-style `for (;;)`
  is missing.

# Safety & Validation

Three levels of runtime validation. Choose per-file or per-function.

```tjs:inline
safety inputs

/#
## The Problem

JavaScript functions silently accept wrong types:

    function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}!` }
    greet(42)  // "Hello, 42!" — no error, just wrong

TypeScript catches this at compile time but the checks
vanish at runtime. Production gets no protection.

## TJS Safety Levels

The `safety` directive sets the default for the whole file:

| Directive | Validates | Use case |
|-----------|-----------|----------|
| `safety none` | Nothing | Metadata only, zero overhead |
| `safety inputs` | Function inputs | Default — catches bad callers |

Per-function overrides:
- `!` = unsafe (skip validation): `function fast(! x: 0) { }`
- `:?` on the return = check what the function returns,
  at runtime: `function f(x: 0):? 0 { }`
#/

// --- Input validation catches bad callers ---

function sayHello(name: 'World'): 'Hello, World!' {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`
}

test 'valid input works normally' {
  expect(sayHello('Alice')).toBe('Hello, Alice!')
}

test 'wrong type returns an error, not garbage' {
  const result = sayHello(42)
  // Not "Hello, 42!" — an actual error value
  expect(result instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}

test 'null returns an error' {
  const result = sayHello(null)
  expect(result instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}

// --- Numeric narrowing catches subtle bugs ---

function setAge(age: +0): +0 {
  return age
}

test 'positive integer accepted' {
  expect(setAge(25)).toBe(25)
}

test 'negative rejected' {
  expect(setAge(-1) instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}

test 'float rejected (age must be integer)' {
  expect(setAge(25.5) instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}

// --- Unsafe functions skip validation (fast path) ---

function fastAdd(! a: 0, b: 0): 0 {
  return a + b
}

test 'unsafe function skips checks (trusted callers only)' {
  expect(fastAdd(3, 4)).toBe(7)
  // No type error even with wrong type — validation skipped
  expect(fastAdd('a', 'b')).toBe('ab')
}

// --- Errors propagate through function chains ---

function cleanName(name: ''): '' {
  return name.trim()
}

function upperCase(name: ''): '' {
  return name.toUpperCase()
}

test 'errors propagate automatically' {
  // cleanName(42) returns error -> upperCase receives error -> returns error
  const result = upperCase(cleanName(42))
  expect(result instanceof Error).toBe(true)
}

test 'valid input flows through the chain' {
  expect(upperCase(cleanName('alice'))).toBe('ALICE')
}

// --- Try without catch: convert exceptions to errors ---

function parseJSON(s: '{}'):! {} {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(s)
  }
}

test 'valid JSON parses normally' {
  const result = parseJSON('{"ok":true}')
  expect(result.ok).toBe(true)
}

test 'invalid JSON returns error instead of throwing' {
  const result = parseJSON('not json')
  expect(result instanceof Error).toBe(true)
  // No try/catch needed by the caller!
}

console.log('Valid:', sayHello('World'))
console.log('Invalid:', sayHello(42))
console.log('Parse ok:', parseJSON('{"x":1}'))
console.log('Parse bad:', parseJSON('nope'))
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

**A bad argument produces a value, not an exception.** `sayHello(42)` does not print
`Hello, 42!` and does not throw: it returns a `MonadicError` describing what was expected,
what arrived, and where (`Expected string for '…sayHello.name', got number`). Your program
keeps running, and the error is something you can inspect, log, or return.

**Errors flow through typed functions.** When a function with typed parameters receives a
`MonadicError` as an argument, it does not run its body; it hands the error back. That is why
`upperCase(cleanName(42))` needs no check between the two calls: the first failure travels to
the end of the chain, carrying its original message. You check once, where you finally use
the result.

**The example decides how strict the check is.** `age: +0` accepts `25` and refuses both `-1`
and `25.5`. You get "non-negative integer" without writing a validator, because that is what
the example `+0` says.

**`!` turns validation off for one function.** `fastAdd('a', 'b')` returns `'ab'`, because
`!` told TJS to trust its callers. Use it on hot internal functions whose inputs were already
checked at the boundary, never on functions that receive outside data.

**`try` without `catch` converts exceptions into values.** `JSON.parse` throws on bad input;
wrapped in a bare `try { }`, the function returns a `MonadicError` instead, so the caller
handles bad JSON the same way it handles a bad argument.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Checking returns as well

Input checks catch bad *callers*. To catch your own bugs, check what a function returns with
`:?`. (A plain `:` return annotation is a worked example that runs as a test at transpile time;
`:!` declares the return type without a test; `:?` runs the test *and* validates every return
at runtime.)

```tjs:inline
function average(xs: [0.0]):? 0.0 {
  if (xs.length == 0) return 'no data' // a bug: a string where a number belongs
  return xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / xs.length
}

console.log('average([2, 4]):', average([2, 4]))

const r = average([])
console.log('average([]):    ', r instanceof Error ? r.message : r)
```

The bad path is caught where it happens, with the function's name in the message, rather
than three calls later as a `NaN`.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Class methods and constructors are checked too

Typed parameters on a constructor or a method validate exactly as a function's do, so a class
cannot be built from, or fed, the wrong kind of value:

```tjs:inline
class Account {
  constructor(owner: 'Ada', balance: 0.0) {
    this.owner = owner
    this.balance = balance
  }

  deposit(amount: 0.0) {
    this.balance += amount
    return this.balance
  }
}

const acct = Account('Ada', 10)
console.log('deposit(5):    ', acct.deposit(5))

const bad = acct.deposit('5')
console.log("deposit('5'):  ", bad instanceof Error ? bad.message : bad)

const nobody = Account(42, 0)
console.log('Account(42, 0):', nobody instanceof Error ? nobody.message : nobody)
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## Gotchas

- **A returned error is easy to ignore.** That is the price of not throwing. If you call a
  function for its side effect and drop the result, a failure disappears. The runtime keeps
  a record of every type error regardless; see [Flight Recorder](/error-history/).
- **`!` is all or nothing for the function.** It disables the checks on every parameter. To
  relax just one, give that parameter a looser type (`x: any`) instead.
- **`safety all` and `?`.** The reference also lists `safety all` (check returns everywhere)
  and a `?` parameter marker (force checks under `safety none`). In transpiled code today,
  neither adds a check: `safety all` validates exactly what `safety inputs` does, and `?`
  under `safety none` is ignored. Use `:?` on the returns you want checked.
- **Validation happens at the call.** A typed parameter checks the value when the function is
  called; it does not stop the body from later putting something else in an object it
  returned.
title: Safety & Validation
description: Three levels of runtime validation. Choose per-file or per-function.

# Better Classes

Classes you can call like functions. Multiple constructors.

```tjs:inline
/#
## The Problem

JavaScript requires `new` for classes, but it's easy to forget:

    class Point { constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y } }
    const p = Point(1, 2)  // undefined! No error, just broken.

And you can't have multiple constructors:

    // Want Point(1, 2) AND Point({x: 1, y: 2})? Too bad.

## TJS Classes (on by default)

In native TJS, classes are callable without `new` by default — no directive needed.
Multiple `constructor()` declarations dispatch by signature.
#/

// --- Classes are callable without new ---

class Point {
  constructor(x: 0.0, y: 0.0) {
    this.x = x
    this.y = y
  }

  magnitude() {
    return Math.sqrt(this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y)
  }

  toString() {
    return `(${this.x}, ${this.y})`
  }
}

test 'callable without new' {
  const p = Point(3, 4)
  expect(p instanceof Point).toBe(true)
  expect(p.x).toBe(3)
  expect(p.y).toBe(4)
}

test 'methods work normally' {
  expect(Point(3, 4).magnitude()).toBe(5)
}

// --- Multiple constructors ---

class Color {
  constructor(r: +0, g: +0, b: +0) {
    this.r = r
    this.g = g
    this.b = b
  }

  constructor(hex: '#000000') {
    const n = parseInt(hex.slice(1), 16)
    this.r = (n >> 16) & 255
    this.g = (n >> 8) & 255
    this.b = n & 255
  }

  toString() {
    return `rgb(${this.r}, ${this.g}, ${this.b})`
  }
}

test 'construct from RGB' {
  const c = Color(255, 128, 0)
  expect(c.r).toBe(255)
  expect(c.g).toBe(128)
  expect(c instanceof Color).toBe(true)
}

test 'construct from hex' {
  const c = Color('#ff8000')
  expect(c.r).toBe(255)
  expect(c.g).toBe(128)
  expect(c.b).toBe(0)
  expect(c instanceof Color).toBe(true)
}

test 'both forms produce same result' {
  const a = Color(255, 0, 0)
  const b = Color('#ff0000')
  expect(a.r).toBe(b.r)
  expect(a.g).toBe(b.g)
  expect(a.b).toBe(b.b)
}

console.log('Point:', Point(3, 4).toString(), '  magnitude:', Point(3, 4).magnitude())
console.log('RGB:', Color(255, 128, 0).toString())
console.log('Hex:', Color('#ff8000').toString())
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

**Calling a class constructs it.** `Point(3, 4)` returns a real `Point`: `instanceof` is true,
methods are on the prototype, and `toString()` works. Every class declared in a `.tjs` file
is wrapped this way, so a class can be used anywhere a function can, including as a callback
(`[1, 2, 3].map(Point)` style code works).

**`new` is an error, not an option.** On a class declared in the same file, `new Point(3, 4)`
does not compile. Since the call already constructs, `new` would only be decoration, and
having two spellings for one thing invites the old mistake in reverse. Built-ins are
untouched: `new Set()`, `new Map()` and `new Float32Array(4)` still need their `new`.

<!-- tjs-doc: expect-error -->

```tjs:static
class Point {
  constructor(x: 0.0, y: 0.0) {
    this.x = x
    this.y = y
  }
}

const p = new Point(1, 2) // compile error: drop the `new`
```

**Constructors and methods validate their parameters.** `Color(r: +0, g: +0, b: +0)` refuses
a negative or fractional channel, and a method with typed parameters checks them on every
call. A bad call returns a `MonadicError` rather than an object in a broken state.

**Several constructors, one class.** `Color` can be built from three numbers or from a hex
string. Each constructor is written separately and the class dispatches on the arguments; see
[Polymorphic Constructors](/polymorphic-constructors/) for the rules.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Defaults, subclasses and chaining

A parameter can have both a type and a default (`by: 0 = 1`: an integer, 1 if omitted), and
subclasses are called the same way as their parents:

```tjs:inline
class Counter {
  constructor(start: 0 = 0) {
    this.count = start
  }

  add(by: 0 = 1) {
    this.count += by
    return this
  }
}

class NamedCounter extends Counter {
  constructor(name: 'clicks', start: 0 = 0) {
    super(start)
    this.name = name
  }

  toString() {
    return `${this.name}: ${this.count}`
  }
}

const c = Counter().add().add(5)
console.log('Counter().add().add(5):', c.count)

const n = NamedCounter('visits', 10).add()
console.log(n.toString(), '| instanceof Counter?', n instanceof Counter)

const oops = Counter().add(1.5)
console.log('add(1.5):', oops instanceof Error ? oops.message : oops)

const items = [1, 2, 3].map(Counter)
console.log('as a callback:', items.map((x) => x.count).join(', '))
```

`NamedCounter('visits', 10)` constructs the subclass, `super(start)` runs `Counter`'s
constructor, and `add(1.5)` is refused because `by` is an integer.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Gotchas

- **Only classes declared in `.tjs` are wrapped.** A class imported from a plain JavaScript
  module, an old-style `function` + `prototype` constructor, or a built-in keeps JavaScript's
  rules, so those still need `new`. TypeScript converted with `fromTS` keeps them too, unless
  the file opts into full TJS with `TjsStrict`.
- **A failed construction is a value.** `Color(-1, 0, 0)` returns a `MonadicError`, not a
  `Color`. If you go on to call a method on it, you call it on the error. Check the result, or
  pass it to a function with typed parameters, which passes the error along.
- **Validation covers parameters, not fields.** The checks run when a constructor or method is
  called. Assigning `point.x = 'oops'` afterwards is ordinary JavaScript and is not checked.
title: Better Classes
description: Classes you can call like functions. Multiple constructors.

# LLM Code Generator

LLM writes AsyncJS code from a description (requires llm capability)

<!-- TODO review -->
Because AJS is small and runs safely, a model can write it for you: describe a task, get back a
program you can store, review and run later. This is how a product lets its users (or its own
agents) automate things without being handed a real programming environment. It needs an LLM, so
on this site it prints a message instead of running; run it locally with the host from
[LLM Chat](/llm-chat/).

````ajs:inline
function generateCode({ task = 'Calculate the factorial of n' }) {
  // System prompt with AsyncJS rules and complete example
  let systemContext =
    'You write AsyncJS code. AsyncJS is a subset of JavaScript.\n\nRULES:\n- Functions take a destructured object param: function foo({ a, b })\n- MUST return an object. WRONG: return 42. RIGHT: return { result: 42 }\n- Types by example: fn({ n: 5 }) means required number param with example value 5\n- NO: async, await, new, class, this, var, for, generator functions (function*)\n- Use let for variables, while for loops\n\nEXAMPLE - calculating sum of 1 to n:\nfunction sumTo({ n: 10 }) {\n  let sum = 0\n  let i = 1\n  while (i <= n) {\n    sum = sum + i\n    i = i + 1\n  }\n  return { result: sum }\n}'

  let schema = Schema.response('generated_code', {
    code: '',
    description: '',
  })

  let prompt =
    systemContext +
    '\n\nWrite an AsyncJS function for: ' +
    task +
    '\n\nReturn ONLY valid AsyncJS code in the code field. Must start with "function" and use while loops (not for loops).'

  let response = llmPredict({ prompt, options: { responseFormat: schema } })
  let result = JSON.parse(response)

  // Clean up any markdown fences and fix escaped newlines
  let code = result.code
  code = code.replace(/```(?:javascript|js)?\n?/g, '')
  code = code.replace(/\n?```/g, '')
  code = code.replace(/\\n/g, '\n')
  code = code.replace(/\\t/g, '\t')
  code = code.trim()

  return {
    task,
    code,
    description: result.description,
  }
}
````

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

- **It writes code and stops.** Unlike [LLM Code Solver](/llm-code-solver/), this agent returns
  the source without running it. The host (or a person) decides what happens next: show it,
  test it, store it, or run it in a VM with its own budget.
- **Structured output carries the code.** The model answers in a `{ code, description }` shape,
  so the code arrives in a field rather than mixed into prose; the cleanup only has to deal with
  fences and escaped newlines.
- **"Types by example".** The prompt teaches `function sumTo({ n: 10 })`: in AJS, as in TJS, the
  value after a colon in a parameter is an example, not a type, and the colon makes the
  parameter required. (`n = 10` would make it optional, with a default.)

<!-- TODO review -->
## Checking the result

Generated source is untrusted input. Before running it, transpile it on the host: a transpile
error is a cheap, early "no", and the AST you get back is data you can inspect (which atoms does
it call?) before granting it anything.

```javascript
const { ast } = transpile(run.result.code, { atoms: vm.atoms }) // throws on invalid AJS
const usesNetwork = JSON.stringify(ast).includes('"op":"httpFetch"')
const tested = await vm.run(ast, { n: 5 }, { fuel: 500 }) // no capabilities at all
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## The gotcha

The model has seen far more JavaScript than AJS, so it will reach for `for (;;)`, `switch`,
`class` or `async`. The transpiler names each one as it refuses it. Feeding that message back to
the model for a second attempt fixes most failures, and costs one more model call.

This is how a product lets its users (or its own agents) automate things without being handed a real programming environment. It needs an LLM, so on this site it prints a message instead of running; run it locally with the host from [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/).

# Local Class Extensions

Add methods to built-in types without polluting prototypes

`extend TypeName { ... }` adds methods to existing types like String,
Array, and Number. Methods are rewritten to `.call()` at transpile time
for known types — zero runtime overhead, no prototype pollution.

Think jQuery-like convenience that feels native but can't break anything.

```tjs:static
extend String {
  capitalize() {
    return this[0].toUpperCase() + this.slice(1)
  }

  words() {
    return this.split(/\s+/)
  }

  reverse() {
    return this.split('').reverse().join('')
  }
}

extend Array {
  last() {
    return this[this.length - 1]
  }

  sum() {
    return this.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)
  }
}

extend Number {
  clamp(min: 0.0, max: 0.0) {
    return Math.min(Math.max(this, min), max)
  }
}

test 'string extensions' {
  expect('hello world'.capitalize()).toBe('Hello world')
  expect('foo bar baz'.words()).toEqual(['foo', 'bar', 'baz'])
  expect('abc'.reverse()).toBe('cba')
}

test 'array extensions' {
  expect([1, 2, 3].last()).toBe(3)
  expect([10, 20, 30].sum()).toBe(60)
}

test 'no prototype pollution' {
  expect(typeof String.prototype.capitalize).toBe('undefined')
  expect(typeof Array.prototype.last).toBe('undefined')
}
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

The usual way to give strings a `capitalize()` is to assign to `String.prototype`. That works,
and it changes `String` for every piece of code in the page: your libraries, their libraries,
and any future version of JavaScript that adds a `capitalize` of its own with different
behaviour. (This is how `Array.prototype.flatten` became `flat`: a popular library had already
patched in an incompatible `flatten`.)

An `extend` block gets the convenience without the global change. The methods are collected
into a plain object belonging to this file, and a call such as `'hello'.capitalize()` is
rewritten at transpile time to an ordinary function call with the string as `this`. Nothing is
added to any prototype, which is what the last test checks.

- **Methods use `this`**, exactly as they would on a class. That is why they must be written
  with method syntax (`last() { … }`), never as arrow functions, which have no `this` of their
  own. (An arrow-function member is not reported as an error; it is silently left out.)
- **Parameter examples are documentation here, not checks.** Unlike a function or a class
  method, an extension method does not validate its arguments today: `7.clamp('a', 5)` returns
  `NaN`, not an error. Validate inside the method if it matters.
- **Several `extend` blocks for the same type merge**, so you can group extensions by topic.
- **Extensions are file-local.** Another module, including one you import, never sees them.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Try it

```tjs:inline
extend String {
  shout() {
    return this.toUpperCase() + '!'
  }
}

extend String {
  initials() {
    return this.split(' ').map((w) => w[0]).join('')
  }
}

extend Array {
  last() {
    return this[this.length - 1]
  }
}

console.log('hello'.shout())
console.log('Ada Lovelace'.initials())
console.log([3, 1, 4, 1, 5].last())
console.log('String.prototype touched?', typeof String.prototype.shout != 'undefined')
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## The limit you will hit: only literal receivers are rewritten

Today the rewrite is a source transform, and it recognises the receiver's type only when the
receiver is a **literal**: a quoted string or template literal, an array literal, or a number
literal. A call on a variable is left exactly as written:

<!-- tjs-doc: fragment -->

```tjs:static
const xs = [1, 2, 3]
xs.last() // TypeError at runtime: xs.last is not a function
```

Because no prototype was changed, `xs.last` really does not exist, and the call fails when it
runs (not when it compiles). Until receivers are resolved from their types, use extensions on
literals, or wrap the value in one (`[...xs].last()`, `` `${name}`.shout() ``) and accept the
copy. For values you pass around, an ordinary function (`last(xs)`) is the honest choice.
title: Local Class Extensions

# Safer Code

Ban var, enforce immutability. Zero runtime cost.

```tjs:inline
/#
## var Is Dead

JavaScript's `var` is a footgun:
- Hoists to function scope (not block scope)
- Allows accidental redeclaration
- Leaks out of `for` loops

In native TJS, `var` is a compile error by default — no directive needed.
`const` and `let` work normally.

## const! — Compile-Time Immutability

`const!` declares a binding whose properties can't be mutated.
Unlike `Object.freeze()`, there's **zero runtime cost** —
the check happens at transpile time. The output is plain `const`.

    const! config = { debug: false, port: 8080 }
    console.log(config.port)  // OK — reads are fine
    config.debug = true       // ERROR at transpile time

    const! items = [1, 2, 3]
    items.map(x => x * 2)    // OK — non-mutating methods
    items.push(4)             // ERROR — mutating method

When runtimes support records/tuples, `const!` can emit those.
Until then, the semantics are locked in with zero overhead.
#/

// --- const and let work fine ---
const greeting = 'Hello'
let count = 0
count += 1

// --- const! prevents mutation ---
const! config = { debug: false, port: 8080, host: 'localhost' }

// Reads are fine
console.log('port:', config.port)
console.log('host:', config.host)

// --- const! arrays ---
const! colors = ['red', 'green', 'blue']

// Non-mutating methods work
const upper = colors.map(c => c.toUpperCase())
console.log('uppercase:', upper)

const found = colors.find(c => c === 'green')
console.log('found:', found)

// --- Multiple bindings ---
const! settings = { theme: 'dark', fontSize: 14 }
const mutable = { x: 1 }
mutable.x = 2  // Fine — not const!

console.log('settings.theme:', settings.theme)
console.log('mutable.x:', mutable.x)

test 'const! emits as plain const' {
  // The output JS has no freeze/seal — zero runtime cost
  expect(typeof config).toBe('object')
  expect(config.port).toBe(8080)
}

test 'non-mutating methods work on const!' {
  expect(colors.map(c => c[0])).toEqual(['r', 'g', 'b'])
  expect(colors.filter(c => c !== 'red')).toEqual(['green', 'blue'])
}
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

Everything in this example is checked **when the file is transpiled**, and none of it costs
anything when the program runs: `const!` emits plain `const`, and the rules below are refusals,
not runtime guards. The output is the JavaScript you would have written by hand.

`const!` protects the *binding's contents* from the code in this file. These are all refused
at transpile time, with the line that did it:

<!-- tjs-doc: expect-error -->

```tjs:static
const! limits = { max: 10, retries: 3 }
limits.max = 20 // assignment
```

<!-- tjs-doc: expect-error -->

```tjs:static
const! limits = { max: 10, retries: 3 }
limits.retries += 1 // compound assignment, ++ and -- too
```

<!-- tjs-doc: expect-error -->

```tjs:static
const! queue = [3, 1, 2]
queue.sort() // a mutating method: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill
```

`delete` is refused as well. Non-mutating methods (`map`, `filter`, `find`, `slice`, `concat`)
are fine, because they return new values; to sort a `const!` array, sort a copy:
`[...queue].sort()`.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Things `.tjs` refuses outright

`const!` is something you opt into. A few things are refused in every `.tjs` file, with an
error that names the replacement:

| Refused | Why | Instead |
|---------|-----|---------|
| `var` | function-scoped, hoisted, redeclarable | `const` or `let` |
| `eval(…)` | runs arbitrary code with your privileges | `Eval()`, the sandboxed form |
| `new Date(…)` | mutable and timezone-dependent | `LegacyDate(x)` when you really need one |
| `new` on a class declared in the file | the class is called, not `new`ed | `Point(1, 2)` |

<!-- tjs-doc: expect-error -->

```tjs:static
var total = 0 // compile error: use const or let
```

`var` and `eval` have no escape hatch: like `with` in strict mode, they are gone. `Date` has
one, `LegacyDate(x)`, because some code (a date library, say) genuinely needs the real thing;
spelling it out makes that choice visible in review.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Gotchas

- **`const!` is shallow and follows the name.** It checks writes made *through the binding*:
  `limits.max = 20` is refused. A write one level down (`config.db.port = 1`) is not caught
  today, nor is a write through another name (`const alias = limits; alias.max = 20`), nor a
  function you pass the object to that mutates it. Treat `const!` as a guard against slips in
  this file, not as `Object.freeze`.
- **The check happens at transpile time only.** Nothing stops other modules, or the
  runtime, from mutating the object. If you need a value that cannot change at runtime, freeze
  it and pay for the freeze.
title: Safer Code
description: Ban var, enforce immutability. Zero runtime cost.

# Inline WASM

> New to WASM in TJS? Start with the **[WASM Quick Start](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/docs/WASM-QUICKSTART.md)**.

Write WebAssembly inline — compiled at transpile time, embedded in the output.

```tjs:inline
/#
## The Problem

Using WebAssembly in JavaScript requires:
1. Write WAT or compile from C/Rust
2. Load a separate .wasm file
3. Instantiate the module async
4. Marshal data between JS and WASM heaps

TJS does all of this for you. Write WASM inline using JS-like
syntax, it compiles at transpile time and embeds as base64.

## Syntax

    function fast(x: 0, y: 0) {
      wasm {
        // JS-like syntax compiled to WASM bytecode
      } fallback {
        // JS fallback if WASM unavailable
        return x + y
      }
    }

    // Or with a return value:
    function compute(x: 0) {
      return wasm {
        return x * x + 1
      } fallback {
        return x * x + 1
      }
    }

The enclosing function's variables are captured automatically. Numbers
arrive in the block as `f64` (JavaScript-exact); typed arrays annotated
`Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `Int32Array` or `Uint8Array` arrive as
pointers into WASM memory.
#/

// --- Basic: integer math in WASM ---

function addInts(! a: 0, b: 0):! 0 {
  return wasm {
    return a + b
  } fallback {
    return a + b
  }
}

function factorial(! n: 0):! 0 {
  return wasm {
    let result = 1
    for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
      result = result * i
    }
    return result
  } fallback {
    let result = 1
    for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++) result *= i
    return result
  }
}

// --- Float math ---

function lerp(! a: 0.0, b: 0.0, t: 0.0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    return a + (b - a) * t
  } fallback {
    return a + (b - a) * t
  }
}

// --- Array processing ---

function sumArray(! arr: Float32Array, len: 0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    let sum = 0.0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
      let off = i * 4
      sum = sum + f32x4_extract_lane(f32x4_load(arr, off), 0)
    }
    return sum
  } fallback {
    let sum = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) sum += arr[i]
    return sum
  }
}

console.log('addInts(3, 4):', addInts(3, 4))
console.log('factorial(10):', factorial(10))
console.log('lerp(0, 100, 0.25):', lerp(0.0, 100.0, 0.25))
console.log('sumArray([1,2,3,4]):', sumArray(new Float32Array([1, 2, 3, 4]), 4))
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What the example shows

A `wasm { }` block sits inside an ordinary TJS function. The transpiler compiles the block to
WebAssembly bytecode **when the file is transpiled**, embeds the bytes in the emitted
JavaScript, and replaces the block with a call into the compiled module. There is no `.wasm`
file to ship, no build step to add, and no async loading for you to write: inline blocks
instantiate synchronously when the file loads, so the first call already runs in WASM.

Things to notice:

- **The block can `return` a value**, and the function returns it with `return wasm { … }`.
  There is no implicit last-expression return: a block that ends in a bare expression
  returns nothing.
- **Variables are captured, not declared.** `a`, `b`, `n`, `arr` and `len` are the outer
  function's parameters. The transpiler sees which ones the block uses and passes them in.
- **`let` inside the block is typed by its initializer.** `let result = 1` is an `i32`,
  which is what a loop counter wants; `let sum = 0.0` is an `f64`.
- **Every function is marked `!`.** That skips TJS's runtime validation of the outer
  function's parameters, which is usually what you want on a hot path. Without it, scalar
  parameters such as `len: 0` are checked at the call (a fractional `len` returns a
  `MonadicError`), but a `Float32Array` annotation is not a runtime type: the transpiler
  warns that it is unchecked.
- **`fallback { }` is ordinary TJS.** It runs only when the runtime cannot run WASM at all
  (no `WebAssembly`, as in iOS Lockdown Mode, or a refused instantiation). Each such fallback
  is recorded once in `__tjs.records({ source: 'wasm' })`.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Checking the block against its fallback

A block and its fallback should give the same answer, and you can make the runtime prove it.
Setting `globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled = false` forces every block to run its fallback, even
though the WASM is loaded: an A/B switch for testing and benchmarking.

```tjs:inline
function mean(! xs: Float32Array, len: 0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    let sum = 0.0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
      sum = sum + xs[i]
    }
    return sum / len
  } fallback {
    let sum = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) sum += xs[i]
    return sum / len
  }
}

// `/` is JavaScript's division in a block, even between two i32 values
function sevenHalves(! n: 0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    let k = 7
    return k / 2 + n
  }
}

const xs = new Float32Array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
console.log('mean, in WASM:     ', mean(xs, 5))

globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled = false
console.log('mean, in fallback: ', mean(xs, 5))
delete globalThis.__tjs_wasm_enabled

console.log('7 / 2 in a block:  ', sevenHalves(0))
```

`xs[i]` reads an element directly: typed-array element access works inside a block for any
parameter annotated `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `Int32Array` or `Uint8Array`. The
`sevenHalves` function has no `fallback`; that is allowed, and when WASM is unavailable the
transpiler's implicit fallback runs the same body as JavaScript.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

A `wasm { }` body is a small, typed subset of JavaScript, not arbitrary code. Anything outside
it is a **compile error** that names the construct; it is never silently shipped as
JavaScript, because writing `wasm { }` is a request for WASM.

- **Allowed:** numeric `let`, `for` loops (nested, with `break` and `continue`), `if`/`else`,
  `&&`/`||`, arithmetic and comparison, typed-array element access, the `f32x4_*` SIMD
  intrinsics, and the math intrinsics `Math.sqrt`, `abs`, `floor`, `ceil`, `trunc`, `min`
  and `max`.
- **Not allowed:** `while` (use `for`), function calls other than those intrinsics, closures,
  objects, strings, `try`/`catch`, and any allocation. `Math.sin`, `cos`, `log`, `exp` and
  `pow` have no WebAssembly instruction, so a block that uses them does not compile.
- **`%` and the bitwise operators need `i32` operands.** Parameters arrive as `f64`, so
  `x % 2` on a captured number does not compile. For integer algorithms, use a
  [`wasm function`](/wasm-functions/) with `i32` parameters.
- **`==` and `!=` are JavaScript's inside a block**, not TJS's: `x != x` is true for NaN.

<!-- tjs-doc: expect-error -->

```tjs:static
function wave(! t: 0.0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    return Math.sin(t)  // compile error: Math.sin has no WASM instruction
  }
}
```

When should you reach for a block at all? When a profiler says a numeric inner loop is hot.
Most code is faster written plainly; WASM pays off on tight loops over typed arrays, and most
of all with SIMD, which the next chapter covers. [`DOCS-WASM.md`](/DOCS-WASM/) is the full
reference.

# WASM SIMD

> New to WASM in TJS? Start with the **[WASM Quick Start](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/docs/WASM-QUICKSTART.md)**.

Process 4 floats per instruction. No setup, no toolchain.

```tjs:inline
/#
## SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data

SIMD processes 4 float values per instruction — a 4x throughput
improvement for vectorized math. TJS provides SIMD via `f32x4_*`
intrinsics that compile directly to WASM SIMD opcodes.

### Available Intrinsics

| Intrinsic | Operation |
|-----------|-----------|
| `f32x4_load(arr, offset)` | Load 4 floats from array |
| `f32x4_store(arr, offset, vec)` | Store 4 floats to array |
| `f32x4_splat(value)` | Fill all 4 lanes with one value |
| `f32x4_add(a, b)` | Add 4 pairs |
| `f32x4_sub(a, b)` | Subtract 4 pairs |
| `f32x4_mul(a, b)` | Multiply 4 pairs |
| `f32x4_div(a, b)` | Divide 4 pairs |
| `f32x4_neg(a)` | Negate 4 values |
| `f32x4_sqrt(a)` | Square root of 4 values |
| `f32x4_min(a, b)` / `f32x4_max(a, b)` | Lane-wise minimum / maximum |
| `f32x4_eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `gt`, `le`, `ge` | Compare 4 pairs, giving a lane mask |
| `f32x4_select(mask, a, b)` | `a` where the mask is set, else `b` |
| `f32x4_extract_lane(vec, lane)` | Get one float (0-3) |
| `f32x4_replace_lane(vec, lane, val)` | Set one float |
#/

// --- Scale an array by a constant (SIMD: 4 elements per step) ---

function scale(! arr: Float32Array, len: 0, factor: 0.0) {
  wasm {
    let s = f32x4_splat(factor)
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let v = f32x4_load(arr, off)
      f32x4_store(arr, off, f32x4_mul(v, s))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) arr[i] *= factor
  }
}

// --- Dot product (sum of element-wise products) ---

function dot(! a: Float32Array, b: Float32Array, len: 0):! 0.0 {
  return wasm {
    let acc = f32x4_splat(0.0)
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let va = f32x4_load(a, off)
      let vb = f32x4_load(b, off)
      acc = f32x4_add(acc, f32x4_mul(va, vb))
    }
    // Sum the 4 lanes
    return f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 0)
      + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 1)
      + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 2)
      + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 3)
  } fallback {
    let sum = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) sum += a[i] * b[i]
    return sum
  }
}

// --- Demo ---

const SIZE = 1024

// Create test arrays
const arr = new Float32Array(SIZE)
const a = new Float32Array(SIZE)
const b = new Float32Array(SIZE)

for (let i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) {
  arr[i] = i + 1
  a[i] = 1.0
  b[i] = 2.0
}

// Scale
scale(arr, SIZE, 0.5)
console.log('scale([1..1024], 0.5) first 4:', arr[0], arr[1], arr[2], arr[3])

// Dot product: 1.0 * 2.0 * 1024 = 2048
const d = dot(a, b, SIZE)
console.log('dot([1,1,...], [2,2,...], 1024):', d)

// Benchmark
// Measure per-op time by running until at least minMs of wall clock has elapsed,
// then dividing. Timing a single sub-millisecond pass does not work: Firefox clamps
// `performance.now()` to ~1ms for fingerprinting resistance, so a fast result reads
// as 0.00ms — and on hardware faster than whatever the iteration count was tuned for,
// a fixed count drifts back under the clock all by itself.
function timePerOp(fn, minMs = 25) {
  let iters = 0
  const start = performance.now()
  do {
    fn()
    iters++
  } while (performance.now() - start < minMs)
  return (performance.now() - start) / iters
}

const perOp = timePerOp(() => scale(arr, SIZE, 1.001))
console.log(`scale on ${SIZE} floats: ${(perOp * 1000).toFixed(1)}us per op`)
console.log(`  (${(SIZE / perOp / 1000).toFixed(1)} million floats/sec)`)
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What the example shows

An `f32x4` value is a 128-bit WebAssembly SIMD register holding four 32-bit floats, called
**lanes**. Every `f32x4_*` intrinsic works on all four lanes at once, so a loop that steps
`i += 4` does a quarter of the iterations a scalar loop would.

Read the loops with three things in mind:

- **Offsets are in bytes, indexes are in elements.** `f32x4_load(arr, off)` takes a byte
  offset, and a float is 4 bytes, hence `let off = i * 4`. Getting this wrong usually does not
  fail loudly: it reads the wrong floats.
- **`f32x4_splat` builds a constant once, outside the loop.** `scale` multiplies every group
  of four by the same four-lane `s`.
- **A reduction ends with a horizontal sum.** `dot` accumulates four partial sums in one
  register, then adds the four lanes with `f32x4_extract_lane` and returns the total. The
  block must `return` it: a trailing expression on its own returns nothing.

The benchmark at the end runs `scale` repeatedly for at least 25ms and divides, because a
single sub-millisecond call is below the resolution some browsers give `performance.now()`.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Branch-free decisions: compare, mask, select

SIMD has no per-lane `if`. Instead a comparison produces a **mask** (all ones in each lane
where it is true, all zeros where it is false), and `f32x4_select(mask, a, b)` picks from `a`
or `b` lane by lane. `f32x4_min` and `f32x4_max` cover the common case of clamping.

```tjs:inline
// Clamp every value into [0, 1], four lanes at a time
function clamp01(! xs: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  wasm {
    let lo = f32x4_splat(0.0)
    let hi = f32x4_splat(1.0)
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let v = f32x4_load(xs, off)
      f32x4_store(xs, off, f32x4_min(f32x4_max(v, lo), hi))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) xs[i] = Math.min(Math.max(xs[i], 0), 1)
  }
}

// Replace negatives with zero using a lane mask and select
function relu(! xs: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  wasm {
    let zero = f32x4_splat(0.0)
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let v = f32x4_load(xs, off)
      let negative = f32x4_lt(v, zero)
      f32x4_store(xs, off, f32x4_select(negative, zero, v))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) if (xs[i] < 0) xs[i] = 0
  }
}

const a = new Float32Array([-0.5, 0.25, 0.75, 1.5, 2, -3, 0.5, 1])
clamp01(a, a.length)
console.log('clamp01:', Array.from(a).join(', '))

const b = new Float32Array([-1, 2, -3, 4, 5, -6, 7, -8])
relu(b, b.length)
console.log('relu:   ', Array.from(b).join(', '))

// Length 6 is not a multiple of 4: run SIMD on the first 4, finish the tail in JS
const c = new Float32Array([-1, 2, -3, 4, -5, 6])
const whole = c.length - (c.length % 4)
relu(c, whole)
for (let i = whole; i < c.length; i++) if (c[i] < 0) c[i] = 0
console.log('relu with a tail:', Array.from(c).join(', '))
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

- **Lengths must be a multiple of 4.** A SIMD loop reads and writes four floats per step, and
  there is no automatic tail loop. Either pad your arrays (zeros are harmless in a sum or a
  dot product) or finish the last one to three elements in JavaScript, as the last lines
  above do.
- **SIMD loads need a typed array.** Annotate the parameter `Float32Array`. A plain array, or
  a parameter typed by an example such as `[0.0]`, is not a pointer into WASM memory, and a
  SIMD load from it does not compile.
- **Only `f32x4`.** There are no integer or `f64x2` lane types yet.
- **SIMD is a baseline requirement.** All current browsers, Node and Bun support WebAssembly
  SIMD; where it is missing, the `fallback` runs and the event is recorded in
  `__tjs.records({ source: 'wasm' })`.

Copying a regular `Float32Array` into WASM memory and back on every call costs time too. The
next chapter, [WASM Memory](/wasm-memory/), shows how `wasmBuffer()` removes that copy.

# WASM Memory

> New to WASM in TJS? Start with the **[WASM Quick Start](https://github.com/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/blob/main/docs/WASM-QUICKSTART.md)**.

Zero-copy arrays and automatic data marshaling between JS and WASM.

```tjs:inline
/#
## How Data Moves Between JS and WASM

The #1 WebAssembly question: "How do I get my data into WASM?"
TJS handles it automatically. Three modes:

### 1. Scalars — pass through
`i32`, `f32`, `f64` go directly as WASM parameters. No marshaling.

### 2. Regular typed arrays — transparent copy
Pass a normal `Float32Array` and TJS copies it into WASM memory
before the call, then copies results back out after. You don't
have to think about it.

### 3. `wasmBuffer()` — zero-copy shared memory
Allocate directly in WASM memory. Both JS and WASM see the same
bytes. No copy in, no copy out. Mutations are instantly visible.

    const xs = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, 50000)
    xs[0] = 3.14        // JS writes to WASM memory
    wasmFunction(xs)     // WASM reads/writes the same memory
    console.log(xs[0])   // JS sees WASM's mutations immediately

### Supported types
`Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `Int32Array`, `Uint8Array`

### How it works internally
All WASM blocks in a file share one `WebAssembly.Memory` (64MB).
`wasmBuffer` is a bump allocator — it hands out slices of this memory.
When a typed array argument's `.buffer === wasmMemory.buffer`, the
wrapper skips the copy and passes the byte offset directly.
#/

// --- Regular arrays: transparent copy ---

function addOne(! arr: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  wasm {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let v = f32x4_load(arr, off)
      let ones = f32x4_splat(1.0)
      f32x4_store(arr, off, f32x4_add(v, ones))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) arr[i] += 1
  }
}

// Regular Float32Array — TJS copies in before, copies out after
const regular = new Float32Array([10, 20, 30, 40])
addOne(regular, 4)
console.log('Regular array after WASM:', Array.from(regular))
// [11, 21, 31, 41] — changes visible in JS

// --- wasmBuffer: zero-copy shared memory ---

const shared = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, 4)
shared[0] = 100
shared[1] = 200
shared[2] = 300
shared[3] = 400

addOne(shared, 4)
console.log('wasmBuffer after WASM:', Array.from(shared))
// [101, 201, 301, 401] — zero copy, same memory

// --- Practical: large array processing ---

const SIZE = 10000
const data = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, SIZE)
for (let i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) data[i] = i * 0.01

// Process in WASM — no marshaling overhead
function normalize(! arr: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  wasm {
    // Find max (scalar — SIMD max needs horizontal reduction)
    let max = 0.0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) {
      let off = i * 4
      let v = f32x4_extract_lane(f32x4_load(arr, off), 0)
      if (v > max) { max = v }
    }
    // Scale to [0, 1]
    if (max > 0.0) {
      let inv = f32x4_splat(1.0 / max)
      for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
        let off = i * 4
        f32x4_store(arr, off, f32x4_mul(f32x4_load(arr, off), inv))
      }
    }
  } fallback {
    let max = 0
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) if (arr[i] > max) max = arr[i]
    if (max > 0) for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) arr[i] /= max
  }
}

// Measure per-op time by running until at least minMs of wall clock has elapsed,
// then dividing. Timing a single sub-millisecond pass does not work: Firefox clamps
// `performance.now()` to ~1ms for fingerprinting resistance, so a fast result reads
// as 0.00ms — and on hardware faster than whatever the iteration count was tuned for,
// a fixed count drifts back under the clock all by itself.
function timePerOp(fn, minMs = 25) {
  let iters = 0
  const start = performance.now()
  do {
    fn()
    iters++
  } while (performance.now() - start < minMs)
  return (performance.now() - start) / iters
}

// Re-fill each pass: normalize() mutates `data`, and normalizing already-normalized
// data is a different (cheaper) workload — timing it would measure the wrong thing.
const perOp = timePerOp(() => {
  for (let i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) data[i] = i * 0.01
  normalize(data, SIZE)
})
console.log(`Normalized ${SIZE} floats in ${(perOp * 1000).toFixed(1)}us per pass`)
console.log('First 4:', data[0].toFixed(4), data[1].toFixed(4), data[2].toFixed(4), data[3].toFixed(4))
console.log('Last:', data[SIZE - 1].toFixed(4))
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What the example shows

WebAssembly code can only read and write its own **linear memory**, one flat block of bytes.
A JavaScript `Float32Array` normally lives somewhere else, so before a WASM call can see your
data, it has to be put into that memory. TJS does the moving for you, in one of two ways:

- **A regular typed array is copied.** `addOne(regular, 4)` copies `regular` into WASM
  memory, runs the block, and copies the result back. You see the mutation, and you pay for
  two copies on every call.
- **A `wasmBuffer()` array is not copied.** `wasmBuffer(Float32Array, 4)` returns an ordinary
  `Float32Array` whose bytes *are* WASM memory. When one is passed in, the wrapper notices
  that its `.buffer` is the WASM memory and hands over the byte offset instead.

The two calls print the same kind of result. The difference is cost, and it grows with the
array: copying 4 floats is nothing, copying 10,000 floats twice per call can cost more than
the arithmetic. That is why the large `normalize` example allocates `data` with `wasmBuffer`.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Allocate once, reuse forever

`wasmBuffer` is a **bump allocator with no free**: every call hands out a fresh slice of the
one shared memory, and that slice is never returned. This is deliberate. It means nobody has
to decide who owns a buffer or when it dies, even across libraries. The price is that a
`wasmBuffer` call inside a loop, or per request, leaks.

So the pattern is: allocate your working buffers once, when the module loads, and refill
them. A kernel that produces an array takes an **output parameter** rather than allocating
one, so the caller decides where the result goes.

```tjs:inline
// Allocate the working buffers ONCE, when the module loads.
const LEN = 8
const src = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, LEN)
const dst = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, LEN)

// The kernel reads one buffer and writes another; it never allocates.
function squares(! input: Float32Array, output: Float32Array, len: 0) {
  wasm {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i += 4) {
      let off = i * 4
      let v = f32x4_load(input, off)
      f32x4_store(output, off, f32x4_mul(v, v))
    }
  } fallback {
    for (let i = 0; i < len; i++) output[i] = input[i] * input[i]
  }
}

// Each "request" refills the same buffers instead of allocating new ones.
for (const start of [1, 10, 100]) {
  for (let i = 0; i < LEN; i++) src[i] = start + i
  squares(src, dst, LEN)
  console.log(`squares from ${start}:`, Array.from(dst).join(', '))
}

// A regular Float32Array still works: it is copied in, and copied back out.
const plainOut = new Float32Array(LEN)
squares(src, plainOut, LEN)
console.log('into a plain Float32Array:', Array.from(plainOut).join(', '))
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

- **The memory is finite.** All the WASM in one file shares one `WebAssembly.Memory` of 64MB,
  and `wasmBuffer` slices are permanent. Budget for your largest working set, once.
- **Supported element types** are `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `Int32Array` and
  `Uint8Array`.
- **A plain JavaScript array is not a typed array.** `[1, 2, 3]` or a parameter typed by the
  example `[0.0]` has no bytes to share. Annotate kernel parameters as typed arrays and pass
  typed arrays.
- **WASM never allocates.** Neither an inline block nor a `wasm function` can create an array;
  JavaScript allocates every byte. That is the rule that makes the bump allocator safe.

The copy path is not wrong, only slower, and for a small array called rarely it is the
simpler choice. Reach for `wasmBuffer` when the array is large or the call is hot.

# WASM Functions (reusable kernels)

Top-level `wasm function` declarations — the building block for cross-file WASM libraries.

```tjs:inline
/#
## `wasm function` — reusable WebAssembly kernels

Inline `wasm { ... }` blocks live inside a specific JS function. They're
convenient for one-off accelerations but they're not reusable.

`wasm function NAME(...)` at module scope is the reusable form:

- Declared at top level with explicit parameters and return type
- Compiles into the file's single `WebAssembly.Module`
- Other files can `import { NAME } from '...'` (cross-file composition,
  via the moduleLoader path)
- Same source produces both "composed" (tjs-to-tjs) and "boundary" (.js)
  distribution forms — see DOCS-WASM.md

Parameters use WASM type names (`i32`, `f64`, `Float32Array`, etc.), not
TJS example-based syntax. Return types must be `f64` or omitted in v1.
#/

// A scalar dot product — for educational reference.
// Real production code would use the SIMD version below.
wasm function dot_scalar(a: Float32Array, b: Float32Array, n: i32): f64 {
  let acc = 0.0
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    acc = acc + a[i] * b[i]
  }
  return acc
}

// SIMD f32x4 version — processes 4 elements per instruction
wasm function dot_simd(a: Float32Array, b: Float32Array, n: i32): f64 {
  let acc = f32x4_splat(0.0)
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 4) {
    let off = i * 4
    let av = f32x4_load(a, off)
    let bv = f32x4_load(b, off)
    acc = f32x4_add(acc, f32x4_mul(av, bv))
  }
  return f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 0)
    + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 1)
    + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 2)
    + f32x4_extract_lane(acc, 3)
}

// Both functions are now callable from JS. The transpiler emits a wrapper:
//   function dot_scalar(a, b, n) { return globalThis.__tjs_wasm_dot_scalar(a, b, n) }
// that handles type marshaling automatically. Float32Array args use a
// zero-copy fast path when allocated via wasmBuffer().

// Demo: build two random vectors and compare the two implementations
const N = 128
const a = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, N)
const b = wasmBuffer(Float32Array, N)
for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
  a[i] = Math.random()
  b[i] = Math.random()
}

const scalarResult = dot_scalar(a, b, N)
const simdResult = dot_simd(a, b, N)

console.log('dot_scalar:', scalarResult.toFixed(4))
console.log('dot_simd:  ', simdResult.toFixed(4))
console.log('match:     ', Math.abs(scalarResult - simdResult) < 1e-3)

// The real version of this lives in tjs-lang/linalg — just `import { dot }`
// and you get the same SIMD kernel, ready to use.
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What the example shows

An inline `wasm { }` block is part of one JavaScript function: it captures that function's
variables and nothing else can call it. A `wasm function` is a kernel in its own right. It is
declared at module scope with explicit WebAssembly types, compiled into the file's single
`WebAssembly.Module`, and replaced in the output by a plain JavaScript wrapper, so callers
cannot tell it from any other function.

Things to notice:

- **Parameters use WebAssembly type names.** `n: i32` is a 32-bit integer and `x: f64` a
  double; `a: Float32Array` is a pointer into WASM memory, marshaled by the wrapper. TJS
  example values do not work here: inside a `wasm function`, `n: 0` is not an example.
- **The return type is `f64` or nothing.** `i32`, `f32` and `v128` return annotations are
  parsed but the backend always returns `f64`, which reaches JavaScript as an ordinary number.
- **There is no `fallback`.** A `wasm function` is pure WASM. If the runtime cannot run WASM,
  there is no JavaScript path to fall back to, so use an inline block when you need one.
- **`wasmBuffer` arrays skip the copy.** `a` and `b` are allocated in WASM memory, so the
  wrapper passes their offsets instead of copying 128 floats in on every call.

The two implementations agree to within rounding. They are not bit-identical: the SIMD
version adds the products in four interleaved partial sums, and floating-point addition is
not associative.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Integers with WebAssembly semantics

`i32` parameters are where a `wasm function` does something a block cannot. Inline blocks
are JavaScript-exact (numbers arrive as `f64`), so `%` and the bitwise operators, which need
integers, do not compile there. Declared `i32`, they do, and the arithmetic is WebAssembly's
32-bit arithmetic: the right tool for hashes, checksums and random-number generators, and a
surprise if you expected JavaScript numbers.

```tjs:inline
// i32 parameters have WebAssembly's 32-bit semantics, not JavaScript's
wasm function add32(a: i32, b: i32): f64 {
  return a + b
}

wasm function rem(a: i32, b: i32): f64 {
  return a % b
}

// A tiny integer hash: multiply and add wrap at 32 bits, which is the point
wasm function hash3(a: i32, b: i32, c: i32): f64 {
  let h = 17
  h = h * 31 + a
  h = h * 31 + b
  h = h * 31 + c
  return h
}

// One wasm function may call another in the same file
wasm function sq(x: f64): f64 {
  return x * x
}

wasm function hypot2(a: f64, b: f64): f64 {
  return Math.sqrt(sq(a) + sq(b))
}

console.log('add32(2, 3):         ', add32(2, 3))
console.log('add32(2e9, 2e9):     ', add32(2e9, 2e9), '; JavaScript says', 2e9 + 2e9)
console.log('add32(2.9, 0):       ', add32(2.9, 0), '; the fraction is dropped at the call')
console.log('rem(-7, 2):          ', rem(-7, 2))
console.log('hash3(1, 2, 3):      ', hash3(1, 2, 3))
console.log('hash3(123456789, 2, 3):', hash3(123456789, 2, 3))
console.log('hypot2(3, 4):        ', hypot2(3, 4))
```

The rules for `i32`, measured and pinned by the test suite:

| | `i32` in a `wasm function` | JavaScript |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A fractional argument | truncated at the call: `f(2.5)` sees `2` | `2.5` |
| An argument beyond 32 bits | wraps modulo 2³²: `3e9` arrives as `-1294967296` | `3e9` |
| `+`, `-`, `*` | wrap at 32 bits: `2e9 + 2e9` is `-294967296` | `4000000000` |
| `/` | JavaScript division: `7 / 2` is `3.5` | `3.5` |
| `%` | sign of the dividend: `-7 % 2` is `-1` | `-1` |
| `% 0` | **throws** (WebAssembly traps) | `NaN` |

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits

- **No host calls.** A `wasm function` may call the math intrinsics (`Math.sqrt`, `abs`,
  `floor`, `ceil`, `trunc`, `min`, `max`), the `f32x4_*` intrinsics and other `wasm function`s
  in the same module, and nothing else. `Math.sin` needs JavaScript, so it does not compile.
- **No allocation.** The caller allocates every array; a kernel that produces one takes an
  output parameter.
- **SIMD loops need lengths that are a multiple of 4.** `dot_simd(a, b, 130)` would read past
  the data; pad with zeros.
- **`% 0` traps.** Guard the divisor in JavaScript if it can be zero.

Exported with `export wasm function`, the same declarations become a library other files can
import. [WASM Library: SIMD Linalg](/wasm-library-author/) builds one, and `tjs-lang/linalg`
ships the production version of `dot`.

# Predicate Types

A type that is a **function you can run** — and, because it is verified safe, one that can
also validate, autocomplete, and travel as JSON Schema.

```tjs:inline
/#
## The gap this fills

JSON Schema describes STRUCTURE well and computation not at all. "A string"
it can say. "A valid CSS colour" it cannot — that is `#f00`, `rgb(1 2 3)`,
`color-mix(in oklch, red, blue)` and 148 named keywords, which is a grammar,
not a shape.

So every real schema ends up with a `pattern` that is a bad approximation,
or gives up and says `type: 'string'`.

A **predicate** is the missing half: an ordinary function returning true or
false. The interesting part is not that you can write one — it is what
becomes possible once the toolchain can PROVE the function is safe.

## Verified-safe means three things follow

A predicate cluster is checked to be pure, synchronous and composable: no IO,
no clock, no randomness, no unbounded regex backtracking. Given that proof:

1. **It compiles to native JavaScript** — validation costs a function call,
   not an interpreter.
2. **It can be MINED for completions.** The verifier already knows the
   keyword sets and `startsWith` guards inside the predicate, so autocomplete
   comes from the same source as validation and cannot disagree with it.
3. **It serialises into JSON Schema** as the `$predicate` keyword. Naive
   validators see ordinary structure and ignore it; aware ones run the
   predicate. Progressive enhancement, not a fork.

That last point is the strategic one: types stop being erased annotations and
become portable, executable artifacts. See `docs/type-system-north-star.md`.

## `tjs-lang/css` is this made real

Not a toy — the CSS validators are built from verified predicates, and
`suggestColor` mines its completions from the same predicate that validates.
The suggestions are guaranteed valid because they are run through the
compiled predicate before being offered.
#/

import { isColor, suggestColor } from 'tjs-lang/css'

// --- A predicate is just a function: run it ---
console.log('validation:')
console.log('  #ff0000              ->', isColor('#ff0000'))
console.log('  rebeccapurple        ->', isColor('rebeccapurple'))
console.log('  rgb(255 128 0)       ->', isColor('rgb(255 128 0)'))
console.log('  notacolor            ->', isColor('notacolor'))
console.log('  #gggggg              ->', isColor('#gggggg'))

// --- Completions are MINED from the same predicate that validates ---
// Not a separate hand-maintained list, so the two cannot drift apart.
console.log('\nautocomplete from the same source:')
const forRe = suggestColor('re')
console.log('  "re" ->', forRe.map((s) => s.value).join(', '))

// Every suggestion is run through the compiled predicate before being offered,
// so an invalid completion is not something this API can produce.
const allValid = forRe.every((s) => s.kind !== 'value' || isColor(s.value))
console.log('  all suggestions valid ->', allValid)

test 'the predicate accepts every CSS colour form' {
  expect(isColor('#ff0000')).toBe(true)
  expect(isColor('rebeccapurple')).toBe(true)
  expect(isColor('rgb(255 128 0)')).toBe(true)
}

test 'and rejects near-misses' {
  expect(isColor('notacolor')).toBe(false)
  expect(isColor('#gggggg')).toBe(false)
}

test 'completions come from the predicate, and are all valid' {
  const suggestions = suggestColor('re')
  expect(suggestions.length > 0).toBe(true)
  // The guarantee: mined values are run through the compiled predicate.
  expect(suggestions.every((s) => s.kind !== 'value' || isColor(s.value))).toBe(
    true
  )
}

test 'suggestions are relevant to the prefix' {
  const values = suggestColor('re').map((s) => s.value)
  expect(values).toContain('red')
}
```

<!-- TODO review -->
## What to notice

- **`isColor` is called like any function.** There is no schema object to build and no
  `validate(schema, value)` indirection: a predicate is a value test you can hand to `filter`,
  `every`, a parameter, or a `Type`.
- **`suggestColor` never offers anything `isColor` would reject.** The completions are mined
  out of the predicate's own source (its keyword lists and `startsWith` guards), and each mined
  value is run back through the compiled predicate before it is returned. A hand-maintained
  completion list beside a hand-written validator is two sources of truth; this is one.
- **The import is real library code**, not a stub written for the page. `tjs-lang/css` is
  built entirely from verified predicates, and its `verifyCss()` re-checks every cluster.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Writing your own

You do not need the CSS library to get a predicate type. A `Type` with a `predicate` is one,
and the transpiler runs the predicate-safety verifier over its body when it compiles. This
example is self-contained:

```tjs:inline
Type HexColor {
  description: 'a #rgb or #rrggbb colour'
  example: '#ff0000'
  predicate(x) {
    return (
      typeof x === 'string' &&
      (x.length === 4 || x.length === 7) &&
      x[0] === '#' &&
      x.slice(1).split('').every((c) => '0123456789abcdefABCDEF'.includes(c))
    )
  }
}

// The Type is a parameter type like any other. The return annotation is a
// worked example: swatch('#ff0000') must return exactly this string.
function swatch(color: HexColor): 'swatch #ff0000' {
  return `swatch ${color}`
}

console.log('HexColor.check:')
for (const v of ['#f00', '#ff8800', 'red', '#ggg', 42]) {
  console.log(`  ${JSON.stringify(v).padEnd(10)} -> ${HexColor.check(v)}`)
}

console.log('\nas a parameter type:')
console.log('  swatch("#0af") ->', swatch('#0af'))
const bad = swatch('blue')
console.log(
  '  swatch("blue") ->',
  bad instanceof Error ? 'MonadicError: ' + bad.message : bad
)
```

The predicate iterates with `every` rather than a `for` loop on purpose. A predicate the
verifier can certify (pure, synchronous, no loops, no `await`, no `new`, no IO) compiles to a
fuel-bounded guard, so a pathological input makes it answer `false` instead of hanging your
validation. Write the same check with a `for` loop and it still works, because TJS never
rejects a predicate it cannot verify (that would make legal JavaScript illegal); it simply runs
as an ordinary, unbounded function. Prefer the verifiable style for anything that will see
untrusted data.

<!-- TODO review -->
## Limits worth knowing

- **"Verified" is a promise about your own code, not a sandbox.** Verified predicates compile
  to native JavaScript, and no syntactic check makes native JavaScript safe against a
  *hostile author*. So the JSON-Schema `$predicate` paths (`compilePredicateSchema`,
  `createPredicateEvaluator`) run a predicate source only if the host registered it with
  `trustPredicate` or opted in with `trustAllPredicates`; anything else fails closed. Do not
  accept predicate source from users and expect the verifier to protect you.
- **Regex literals inside a predicate run on tjs-lang's own linear engine**, not the host's,
  so a catastrophic-backtracking pattern cannot hang a certified predicate. That engine has no
  backreferences or lookaround.
- **The first example imports `tjs-lang/css`**, so it needs a host that can resolve that
  package. The `HexColor` example has no imports and runs anywhere.

See [Declarations](/declarations/) for the full `Type` syntax and the
[north-star note](/type-system-north-star/) for where `$predicate` is heading.

  expect(values).toContain('red')
}
description: A type that is a **function you can run** — and, because it is verified safe, one that can also validate, autocomplete, and travel as JSON Schema.
