# Changelog

All notable changes to **tjs-lang** are documented here.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## [Unreleased]

### Fixed

- **A class can construct itself in a static initializer** (#3841). A static field or static
  block runs while the class is being defined, before the callable wrapper exists, so a
  self-call there threw `__tjs_callable is not a function`. That is exactly what graduating a
  converted `static zero = new Money(0)` produced. There, the call now constructs directly.

- **Enum members read as properties, as in TypeScript** (#3840). `Enum` kept its members only
  under `.members`, so a converted TypeScript `enum Color { Red = 'red' }` read `Color.Red` as
  `undefined`: conversion changed what the program did. Members are now properties of the enum
  (`Color.Red`), and numeric members map back to their names (`Dir[0] === 'Up'`), in both the
  inline runtime and `tjs-lang/runtime`. A member named like one of the enum's own fields
  (`check`, `values` …) does not shadow it; `.members` still has it.

- **Infix `Is` / `IsNot` find their operands by structure** (#3830). The operand pattern
  treated parentheses as identifier characters, unbalanced, so `console.log(a Is b)` compiled
  to `Is(console.log(a, b))`: a different program, with no error. `[1, 2] Is [1, 2]` and
  `Point(1, 2) Is Point(1, 2)` did not compile at all. Operands are now postfix chains with
  balanced groups, or bracketed literals. Where another operator touches an operand
  (`1 + a Is b`, `!a Is b`), precedence would decide the meaning, so it is refused with the
  remedy, `Is(a, b)`, instead of guessed.

- **An AJS agent's declared inputs are enforced for every kind of example (BREAKING, toward
  correctness)** (#3835). The input schema covered strings, floats, booleans, lists, objects
  and unions; every other kind became `{}`, which admits anything. So `function f(n: 10)`
  accepted `'x'`, `n: +0` accepted `-1`, and `m: 'a' | 'b'` accepted `'z'`: a declared input
  contract that checked nothing, on the path that runs untrusted code. Now `integer`,
  `{ type: 'integer', minimum: 0 }` and `{ enum: […] }`. Inputs JSON cannot carry (a bigint,
  a function) and regex examples (guest schemas may not hold host patterns) are refused at
  transpile time with the remedy. The schema switch is exhaustive, so a new kind is a compile
  error rather than a silent `{}`. An agent that relied on the hole (`n: 10` called with a
  string) is now refused.

- **`typeof` on an undeclared name is `'undefined'` in native TJS, as in JavaScript** (#3822).
  `typeof x` is rewritten to `TypeOf(x)` (so `typeof null` is `'null'`), and a call evaluates
  its argument, so the feature-detection idiom `typeof window === 'undefined'` threw a
  ReferenceError in a `.tjs` file. A bare identifier now asks JavaScript's own `typeof` first.

- **Generated `.d.ts` keeps `static` and typed defaults on class members** (#3620). The method
  scan matched `name(`, so `static of(…)` lost `static` and was declared an instance method
  (`Box.of(2)` failed with TS2339 in a consumer), and `scale(k: 0 = 1)` was declared a REQUIRED
  `k: any`. Now `static of(v: number)` and `scale(k?: number)`.

- **Graduating a converted file no longer changes what it does** (#1992, #2022, #2040).
  `fromTS` output carries a `tjs <- …` annotation meaning JavaScript semantics; `graduate()`
  removes it and every native-TJS rule switches on. A differential test found nine ways that
  changed behaviour: `'5' == 5` turned false, `typeof null` turned `'null'` (so a
  `typeof v === 'object'` branch skipped null), `f(n = 5)` refused `2.5`, an object-literal
  default started merging, and `var` and `new Date()` made the graduated file fail to compile.
  Conversion now writes each reliance in a spelling that means the same under both semantics:
  `DangerousLegacyEquals(a, b)` (not against `null`, where TJS agrees), `LegacyTypeOf(x)`
  (not where the answer cannot be `'object'`), `LegacyDate(…)`, `n = 5.0`,
  `LegacyDefault({…})`, and `var` hoisted to a `let` at the top of its function (the same
  scoping, closures over a loop variable included). `graduate()` now REFUSES what nothing can
  preserve (`eval`, `new Function`), naming it and returning the input unchanged. The one
  accepted change: truthiness unwraps boxed primitives. `TjsStrict` files are not rewritten.
  **New:** `LegacyTypeOf(x)`, JavaScript's `typeof`, in the family of named escapes.

- **Every named escape works when it is a file's only runtime use.** The emitter's list of what
  needs the inline runtime had `LegacyDate` but not `DangerousLegacyEquals`, `DangerousLegacyNot`,
  `LegacyExactly`, `LegacyNotExactly` or `LegacyDefault`, so a file using only one of those threw
  a ReferenceError. Each is now tested alone, in both dialects.

## [0.14.0-rc.10] — 2026-10-31

On the `rc` dist-tag. Mostly what tosijs-native found building natively in `.tjs` from the
first line: typed parameters with defaults, class methods that validate, `.d.ts` that
compiles across files, a `Bun.build` plugin and an optional shared runtime per bundle. Pin
`0.14.0-rc.10` exactly to test it.

### Read this first: what changes since rc.9

- **Class methods and constructors validate their parameters (BREAKING, toward
  correctness).** `Box('s')` for `constructor(v: 0)` returns a MonadicError. A platform
  callback whose return value is discarded silently skips its body on a refused call:
  `attributeChangedCallback(name = '', old = '', value = '')` refuses the platform's
  `old = null`. Spell `old = null`.
- **`name: Type = default`** works in TJS (#3596), and is REFUSED on the AJS path with a
  remedy, until the type can reach the agent's input schema.
- **A bare `null` default accepts any value** (#3609), as a null dictionary member did.
- **Emitted `__tjs` names a parameter's Type** (`typeName`) and keeps a function type's
  signature; a consumer reading `__tjs` sees more fields.
- **New entry points:** `tjs-lang/bun-build-plugin` (`tjsPlugin()` for `Bun.build`) and
  `tjs-lang/prelude` (with `prelude: 'import'` / `sharedPrelude`; only for a bundle built by
  the same tjs-lang).
- **`tjs emit` rewrites relative `./x.tjs` imports to `./x.js`** (#3592), in the `.js` and
  the `.d.ts`.
- **Doc comments:** `findDocCommentSpans` / `extractDocComments` are exported (#3604), and the
  scan is linear (it was quadratic before fuel on the AJS path).

### Added since rc.9

- **A shared prelude: `prelude: 'import'` and `tjsPlugin({ sharedPrelude: true })`** (#3594,
  from tosijs-native). Every emitted module carries its own inline runtime, so a bundle of N
  modules carried N copies. Opted in, a module instead imports a factory from the new
  `tjs-lang/prelude` and builds its own instance: the code is in the bundle once, the state
  (the `extend` projection table, the call-stack ring) stays per module. The behaviour is the
  inline runtime's, checked by a differential corpus run both ways. A module compiled by a
  different tjs-lang is refused at load, by content hash. Measured on tosijs-native (seven
  modules): 102.6 KB → 72.3 KB raw, one prelude instead of seven; gzip is unchanged
  (15.4 → 15.6 KB), because compression had already been folding the copies. So the win is
  parse size, not transfer. Default output is unchanged and still standalone.
  **This output is for a bundle built by the same tjs-lang**, which is what the plugin does:
  it names an exact prelude, so do not publish `prelude: 'import'` files unless the package
  pins tjs-lang to that exact version. A consumer's tree resolving a different copy gets
  "compiled against prelude X" at load. Signature examples and `test` blocks still run under
  it (they run against the inline form: the rc.10 review found every one inconclusive, so a
  wrong example passed the build).

- **`name: Type = default`** (#3596, from tosijs-native): a type and a separate default,
  TypeScript's spelling. The parameter is checked against the type, optional, and defaults to
  the default; it is how a literal union gets a default (`mode: 'grant' | 'deny' = 'grant'`),
  which no other spelling could express. It was a bare `Unexpected token`. A passed object
  must satisfy the type whole (not merge-on-partial, which stays the untyped `opts = { … }`),
  a literal default that fails its own type is a compile error, and the `.d.ts` declares the
  parameter optional with its type. TypeScript conformance's "param with default" row passes.

- **`tjs-lang/bun-build-plugin`: `tjsPlugin()` for `Bun.build`** (#3593, from tosijs-native).
  `tjs-lang/bun-plugin` is a runtime registration (Bun's `plugin()`), which `Bun.build`
  ignores, so a project bundling `.tjs` had to write its own. `Bun.build({ plugins:
  [tjsPlugin()] })` bundles a `.tjs` graph that runs in plain Node; the preload now uses the
  same plugin.
- **Return examples can run on load, opt-in** (#3599, from tosijs-native): `tjsPlugin({
  runTests: true })`, or `TJS_RUN_TESTS=1` with the preload. A wrong return example (or a
  failing `test` block) then fails the build or the import, instead of passing `bun test` and
  failing only `tjs check`. Off by default, since it runs a file's tests on every load.

- **`findDocCommentSpans` and `extractDocComments` are exported** from `tjs-lang`,
  `tjs-lang/lang` and `tjs-lang/browser` (#3604). They are TJS's own doc-comment grammar
  (`/# … #/`: literal-masked and nestable), so a doc system can read a `.tjs` file's
  documentation the way the language does. tosijs-ui feature-detects them, and a `.tjs` file
  documented the TJS way gets a page.

### Fixed since rc.9

- **Explaining a rejected value costs a bounded multiple of checking it** (#3619, rc.10
  review). The explainer behind "where did it fail" (#3597) asked whether each named Type's
  whole subtree passed before descending into it, so a rejected recursive value cost
  subtree × depth: 37× the accept at depth 60. It now walks the shape first and asks only
  where the walk found nothing (a predicate refusing a well-shaped value), at most 16 times;
  past that it stops explaining and the error keeps its plain message. About 3× the accept at
  any depth or width, counted in property reads. The messages are the old explainer's,
  checked against it over every leaf of a nested config broken nine ways.

- **The doc-comment scan is linear** (rc.10 review). `findDocCommentSpans` (public since
  #3604) and `blankDocComments` run before any fuel on the AJS path, and were quadratic:
  `'/#'.repeat(k)` took 28s at 128 KB, 11.6ms now. The new scan returns exactly the old one's
  spans, checked against the old implementation over 20,000 generated sources, and a
  work-counting row fails if it stops being linear. Exposure was bounded by the 8 KB default
  source cap (about 60ms); a host that raised `maxSourceBytes`, or called `transpile()`
  directly, got super-linear work before any budget.

- **AJS refuses `name: Type = default`, with a remedy** (rc.10 review). The new spelling
  (#3596) reached AJS through the parameter code it shares with TJS and was accepted with the
  type dropped, so `n: number = 5` admitted `'x'` into the agent: a declared input contract
  silently unenforced. rc.9 refused it as a syntax error; it is refused again, now saying
  what to write (`n = 5`), until the AST emitter carries the type into the input schema. The
  AJS construct ratchet lists it, so the next leak through the shared code fails by name.

- **An emitted function's `__tjs` says WHICH named Type a parameter has.** `serializeType`
  copied a fixed field list that left out `typeName`, so a `declared` parameter serialized as
  `{ kind: 'declared' }` and `wrap(fn, fn.__tjs)` reported "named Type 'undefined'". A
  function-typed parameter lost its signature (`params`, `returns`) the same way, and a
  degraded `any` lost its `unresolved` text. The test meant to catch it had been passing on
  another row's record; CI's test order exposed it.

- **The flight recorder's module-level ring mirrors into an installed instance.** With
  `globalThis.__tjs = createRuntime()` (the documented setup), what the runtime module itself
  records, such as a `wrap()` notice, went to a ring nothing read. Instances already mirrored
  into the global; the module recorder was the one sink without. `installRuntime()` (the
  module itself on the global) is skipped, so nothing loops.

- **A bare `null` or `undefined` parameter default means any value** (#3609, from
  tosijs-native): `function render(doc = null)` accepted ONLY null, refusing ordinary
  callers, while a null dictionary member accepted anything. It now means "any value,
  defaulting to null", the usual JavaScript meaning. `doc: null` still means only null.
  **Behaviour change** for code relying on the refusal.

- **A class can call itself from its own body** (#3608): `static of(v) { return Box(v) }`
  threw "Cannot call a class constructor without new". TJS makes a class callable by
  rebinding its outer name to a wrapper; inside the body the name is the raw class. The call
  now goes through the wrapper (recorded on the class as a non-enumerable
  `__tjs_callable`), so overloaded constructors still dispatch. The callee is resolved by
  scope: a method that binds its own `Box` (a local, a destructured or default parameter, an
  inner function, `catch (Box)`, a loop binding) calls its own (rc.10 review: those threw
  `Box.__tjs_callable is not a function`), and whether a class is wrapped is read from the
  wrapper's statements, not from source text a string can spell.
- **A `}` in a string or regex inside a method no longer ends the class** for the
  callable-class wrapper (literal blindness). The wrapper landed inside the class body, where
  it parsed by accident as a class field named after the class, so that class was never made
  callable.

- **A dictionary default may have an `undefined` member** (#3591, from tosijs-native),
  meaning "any value, defaulting to undefined", as a `null` member already did. It was
  refused as "not a clonable literal value", so "absent means use the global" had to be
  spelled `null`. The `.d.ts` declares it `any`.

- **A declared Type's failure says where** (#3597, from tosijs-native). A config type whose
  one bad field was deep inside reported `Expected Config for '…config', got object`; it now
  says `Expected Config for '…config': products[1].kind: expected string, got number`
  (missing members, nested shapes, the integer rule, function members and recursive Types
  included). The explanation runs only after the check has failed, and never throws.
  **Size:** it adds ~1.95KB (~750 bytes gzipped) to each emitted module that names a
  declared Type; sharing one runtime per bundle is #3594.

- **Class methods validate their parameters, the constructor included** (#3598, from
  tosijs-native). **Behaviour change:** a method or constructor with typed parameters now
  returns a MonadicError for a wrong argument (`Box('s')` for `constructor(v: 0)`, which used
  to build a Box with `v = 's'`), as the same signature on a function always did. Methods
  were only stripped of their annotations. Static methods and destructured method
  parameters are covered; a derived constructor's checks run before `super()`, which
  JavaScript allows since they return only on failure. Setters are NOT checked (their return
  value is discarded, so a refusal would silently drop the write), nor is `dialect: 'js'`.
  **BREAKING for platform callbacks whose return value the platform discards.** A refused
  call returns a MonadicError instead of running the body, and the host never looks:
  `attributeChangedCallback(name = '', old = '', value = '')` is called with `old = null` the
  first time an attribute is set, so the body silently does not run. The refusal is recorded
  in the flight recorder (`__tjs.records()`). Spell what the platform actually passes:
  `old = null` (a null default accepts any value), or mark the method `/* unsafe */`.

- **A function-valued member of a Type's example means "a function here"** (#3595, from
  tosijs-native). `Type Bridge { example: { call: (a) => 1 } }` refused every value, one of
  exactly that shape included, in both checkers: the inline one compared a function example
  by identity, and the runtime `Type`'s inference has no schema for a function. Both now
  check `typeof === 'function'` there (a Type, which is also callable, is still a Type).

- **A package written in `.tjs` emits as a package TypeScript and plain Node can use**
  (#3587, #3588, #3589, #2749; found by tosijs-native, the first project written natively in
  `.tjs`). Five defects, each a reason such a package could not be published:
  - a barrel `index.tjs` of `export { … } from './x.tjs'` emitted an EMPTY `index.d.ts`, so
    the package's entry point had no types (re-exports now pass through);
  - a Type imported from another file was declared `any` (it is now named, and imported
    with `import type`);
  - a Type named inside another Type's example was `any[]` (`products: Product[]`);
  - a `null` dictionary-default member, which admits any value at runtime, was declared
    `null`, so a TypeScript caller passing a real value failed to compile (now `any`);
  - `tjs emit` wrote `./x.tjs` imports into the `.js` it emitted beside `x.js`, so the
    output loaded only where a `.tjs` loader was installed. Relative `.tjs` specifiers are
    now rewritten to `.js` in emitted files (JavaScript and `.d.ts`; found by parsing, so a
    mention in a string or comment is untouched), which `moduleResolution: nodenext` also
    requires. The library's `tjs()` keeps source specifiers, since its output runs where
    `.tjs` sources do.
  Pinned end to end: a multi-file package is emitted with the CLI, a consumer is compiled
  against it with TypeScript (`nodenext`, strict, skipLibCheck off), and the `.js` runs in
  plain `node`.

## [0.14.0-rc.9] — 2026-10-28

On the `rc` dist-tag. A VM security fix (#3531), destructured and array-pattern parameters
checked as the one argument they are at any position, `wrap()` working with emitted
metadata, `:?` returns checked like parameters, tosijs proxies seen through everywhere, Type
values as defaults, and sharper error messages. Pin `0.14.0-rc.9` exactly to test it.

### Read this first: what changes since rc.8

- **Published metadata (BREAKING, toward correctness):** a destructured or array-pattern
  parameter beside others is ONE entry in `__tjs.params`, keyed by its binding pattern
  (`{ w, h }, k`, not `w, h, k`); a lone destructured parameter's `__tjs` gains
  `destructured: true`.
- **A `:?` return with a wrong member now returns an error** (#3408).
- **A list element failure names the element** (`f.xs[1].t`), not the list (#3407).
- **`function f(xs = [Book])` takes a list of Types**, not of Books (#3411).
- **`dialect: 'js'` no longer runs return examples** (#3412).

### Security since rc.8

- **The VM's equality runs no host code on the values it compares** (#3531). rc.7's tosijs
  see-through (`unwrapBoxed`) added a property GET of `Symbol.for('xin-value')`, and the VM's
  `==` used it: a GET runs a getter or a Proxy trap, which the VM's equality promises never to
  do. A guest cannot make such a value (guest values are membraned data), but a host object
  returned by an atom tagged `effects: 'pure'`, which skips the membrane, reached the
  comparison and its trap ran, unmetered, inside guest evaluation. The `instanceof` checks it
  replaced also consulted a Proxy's `getPrototypeOf` trap. The VM now unwraps boxed primitives
  by slot reads only (`unwrapBoxedSlots`) and does not see through tosijs proxies, which no
  guest value is. Affected: 0.14.0-rc.7 and rc.8 for the GET; the `instanceof` trap reads are
  older. Not a sandbox escape: the code that ran is the embedder's own object.
  **0.14.0-rc.7 and rc.8 are deprecated on npm** (2026-10-29), pointing at 0.14.0-rc.9 or
  later. No GitHub advisory: a guest program cannot trigger it, only a host object returned
  by an embedder's own `effects: 'pure'` atom.

### Fixed since rc.8

- **A Type in a default is a value: functions can take Types** (#3411). In
  `function shelf(types = [Book])` or `function accepts(t = Book)`, the default is the Type
  itself, and a function may take Types and operate on them. The default was read as an
  EXAMPLE ("a list of Book-shaped values"), so the parameter refused its own default and
  every other Type passed in. A declared Type named in a default (including a
  dictionary default's members) is now checked as a Type (`Expected Type for …` when it is
  not one). The colon form keeps its meaning: `b: [Book]` is a list of Books. **Behaviour change:**
  `function f(xs = [Book])` used to check its argument as a list of Books (and refuse its
  own default); it now takes a list of Types. For a list of Books write `xs: [Book]`.
- **The `.d.ts` declares a parameter with a non-literal default as optional** (`t = Book`,
  `x = now()` were required), and parenthesizes a list of functions (`(() => any)[]`, not
  `() => any[]`).
- **Signature examples run under one condition, at build and in the test runner** (#3412):
  native TJS. Under `dialect: 'js'` the build ran a return example (and failed the
  transpile on a wrong one) while `tjs().testRunner` never did. A return annotation is a
  worked example only in native TJS, so the `js` dialect now runs neither; native TJS still
  runs both. **Behaviour change:** a `dialect: 'js'` source with an inconsistent return
  example now transpiles.
- **tosijs proxies are seen through everywhere a value is checked** (#3406). rc.7 listed three
  places that still refused one: a proxy held inside a plain object or list
  (`{ a: calculator.x }`, `[calculator.x]`), an overloaded function's dispatch (adding an
  overload made `f(calculator.x)` "no matching overload"), and a `:?` return check. Each is
  now checked as the value the proxy wraps, while the body, the chosen overload and the
  caller still receive the proxy itself. Member and element checks pay nothing on the happy
  path (the unwrap runs only after the raw check has failed); dispatch unwraps each argument
  it tests, measured at a few percent on a dispatch-only micro-benchmark. A message names
  the wrapped value's type, not "object".
- **A type error names the contract and the place** (#3407). A member of a named Type said
  `Expected declared`; it says `Expected Book`. A list whose ELEMENT failed said
  `Expected array of object …, got array of object`; it now names the element and, for a
  shape, the member: `Expected string for 'f.xs[1].t', got number` (found on the failure
  path only, carrying the whole list as `received`). A dictionary-default member says
  `array of string`, not `array`. **Message change:** code that matched the old list-level
  wording for an element failure will see the element-level one.
- **A checked return (`:?`) is checked like a parameter** (#3408). **Behaviour change,
  toward correctness:** a `:?` function returning an object with a wrong member now gets an
  error back. Named Types were resolved only for parameters, so `:? Book`, `:? [Book]` and
  `:? { top: Book }` checked nothing; and the return check tested only the outer kind, so
  even `:? { top: 0 }` returned `{ top: 'x' }` unrefused. Both are fixed; a key written
  `key = value` (a return default) may still be absent, `:!` is still the opt-out, and a
  union with a member that cannot be resolved stays unchecked, as for parameters.
- **An array-pattern parameter is one parameter, checked as one** (#3497). `g([a, b], k)`
  had no metadata entry for its array parameter (it listed only `k`), so position-based
  readers misaligned; a TS-style annotation (`[a, b]: [0, 0]`) was erased unchecked, and
  `null` THREW. It is now named, checked as an array (against its annotation when there is
  one), then destructured, like an object pattern (#3443); the `.d.ts` declares it.
- **A `Type` with an object or list example is aliased to its shape in the `.d.ts`** (#3482).
  `export Type R { example: { x: 0, y: 0 } }` was declared `type R = Record<string, any>`, and
  a list example `any[]`, so TypeScript consumers got no member types for any parameter of
  such a Type. The declaration finder's patterns stopped at the first `,` or `}`, and the
  alias was guessed from the example's first character. The example is now read as an
  expression (acorn decides where it ends) and inferred as a parameter's example is:
  `type R = { x: number; y: number }`. Class methods with a list example now agree with
  functions (`string[]`, not `any[]`).
- **Pushing a release tag no longer re-runs the full suite it was attested on** (#3445).
  `release:ready` attests every lane on the tagged tree; the pre-push hook re-ran ~8 minutes
  of suite anyway, git's connection to the remote sat idle until GitHub dropped it, and a
  green hook ended in exit 141 with the tag not pushed. The hook now accepts a valid
  attestation (`scripts/attested.ts`), and says what a 141 means if a long run still ends in
  one.
- **`wrap(fn, fn.__tjs)` works** (#3496). `wrap` is documented to take a function's `__tjs`
  metadata and refused every call given it, `wrap((a, b) => a + b, add.__tjs)(1, 2)`
  included: its `checkType` understood kind names (`'number'`) and Type objects, and emitted
  metadata carries transpiler descriptors (`{ kind: 'integer' }`). `checkType` now checks a
  descriptor strictly, every kind handled. A named `Type` cannot be resolved from metadata
  alone, so it passes and the flight recorder says so once per path. And `wrap` treats a
  single object argument as named parameters only when the metadata says the function
  destructures it: emitted `__tjs` now carries `destructured: true` for a lone destructured
  parameter. It used to GUESS from the call, which read `area(r: { w, h })` called with
  `{ w, h }` as `r: undefined`.
- **The `.d.ts` declares a destructured parameter as one parameter** (#3444).
  `export function area({ w: 0, h: 0 })` was declared `area(w: number, h: number)`, so a
  TypeScript consumer was told to call `area(2, 3)`, which the runtime refuses, and the
  correct `area({ w: 2, h: 3 })` did not type-check. It is now
  `area({ w, h }: { w: number; h: number })`: a member with a default is optional, a
  default for the whole argument makes the parameter optional, and the TypeScript spelling
  keeps its declared type (`({ x }: R)`).
- **A destructured parameter beside others is one parameter, checked as one** (#3443).
  **BREAKING (toward correctness), metadata:** `function area3({ w: 0, h = 2 }, k: 0)` listed
  its parameters as `w, h, k`, flattening the pattern's members in among the positional
  ones, so everything reading `__tjs.params` by position misread it (the `.d.ts` declared
  three parameters; callback-shape checks compared the wrong positions). It is now
  `{ w, h }, k`: one entry, keyed by its binding pattern and typed as the object it
  destructures. A lone destructured parameter's metadata is unchanged (its members, with
  `isDestructuredParam`). The parameter itself now behaves like a lone one: named, checked
  as an object (a monadic error passes through; `null` is a returned error, no longer a
  throw; a failing member carries the object as `received`), then destructured, and the
  TypeScript spelling `(x, { b }: { b: 0 })` is checked in any position instead of erased.
  An ARRAY pattern is now one parameter too (#3497).

## [0.14.0-rc.8] — 2026-10-20

On the `rc` dist-tag. A type error now carries what you passed (`err.received`), destructured
parameters are checked as the one argument they are (in both the TJS and the TypeScript
spelling), converted TypeScript gets native TJS for them, and runtime errors name the right
line again after a declaration block. Pin `0.14.0-rc.8` exactly to test it.

### Read this first: what changes since rc.7

- **A destructured parameter returns an error instead of throwing** for `null` or a missing
  argument, and passes a monadic error through. Code that caught the throw gets a value.
- **`({ w, h }: Shape)` is now checked.** Converted TypeScript under `TjsStrict` that passed
  ill-typed objects to a destructured parameter now gets errors back.
- **AJS refuses `({ a }: T = d)`**, as it already refused `({ a } = d)`. It used to accept it
  and silently drop the default.

### Added since rc.7

- **A type error carries the argument it refused, as `err.received`.** It said only "got
  object", so the receiver could not see what it got: in particular an `Error` the caller
  made, which a typed function refuses (only TJS's own errors pass along) and which was then
  lost. When a member fails, `received` is the whole argument (`{ width: 3 }` for a missing
  `r.height`), not the member's `undefined`: the error is that the thing passed was not a
  rectangle. A destructured parameter (`({ w: 0, h: 0 })`) is the same: see below. `received` is non-enumerable, so logging or `JSON.stringify` of the error never walks
  a large or cyclic value. Set at every site: the inline runtime in emitted code, the global
  and per-instance `typeError`, and the callback-shape checks.
  The refused value is held by the error, so the flight recorder's ring (the last 64
  errors) keeps it reachable until the ring wraps or `__tjs.clearRecords()`; mind that for
  large or sensitive payloads.

### Fixed since rc.7

- **`({ w, h }: Shape)` is checked, and `fromTS` writes native TJS for it where it can**
  (#3434). The TypeScript spelling of a typed destructured parameter had its annotation
  erased, behind a comment claiming it was "captured for metadata"; nothing captured it, so
  `d({ w: 'x' })` returned `NaN`. It is the shape `fromTS` emitted for every typed
  destructured TypeScript parameter, so converted code checked none of them, even under
  `TjsStrict`. Now the argument is checked against `Shape` (an object shape, a named
  `Type`, a union) and then destructured, renames included, and a default written after
  the type (`({ a }: T = {})`) is kept, where it used to be erased along with the type.
  `fromTS` now emits `({ w: 0.0, h: '' | undefined })` for an inline type whose members
  native syntax can hold, and keeps `: Shape` for a named type, a rename or a pattern
  default (in a pattern, `{ w: R }` is a RENAME, so a pattern cannot name a type).
- **A destructured parameter is checked as the argument it destructures** (#3432). It is one
  parameter expecting an object, and now behaves like every other: a monadic error passes
  through unchanged, and anything else that is not an object (`null`, nothing, a string, an
  `Error` you made) is a returned type error carrying it as `received`. Before, the
  destructuring happened in the parameter list, before any check could run: `null` or a
  missing argument THREW ("Cannot destructure"), an error passed in became a new "got
  undefined" error, and a member's failure could not name the object. **BREAKING, toward
  correctness:** code that caught that throw now gets an error value. The emitted function
  takes `__tjs_arg` and destructures it in the body after the checks; `.length`, defaults,
  extra arguments, `this` and `arguments` are unchanged (`dialect: 'js'` is untouched).
- **A runtime type error names the right line after a declaration block** (#3404). A `Type`,
  `Generic`, `FunctionPredicate`, `Union` or `Enum` declaration became one line of output, so
  every line below it moved up: a function on line 5 under a four-line `Type` reported
  `<source>:2:…`. The rewrites now keep the source's line count (`lineKeeper`).

## [0.14.0-rc.7] — 2026-10-19

On the `rc` dist-tag. TJS now works with tosijs models (typed functions, `==`, truthiness and
`given` see through tosijs proxies), live pages check signature examples, list parameters check
their elements, and the TJS book's Part I, "Learn to Program", is complete. Pin
`0.14.0-rc.7` exactly to test it.

### Read this first: what changes since rc.6

- **A list parameter checks every element** against a named `Type` or an object shape
  (`[Book]`, `[{ title: '', pages: 0 }]`). Code that passed a malformed element to one now
  gets an error value back.
- **Checks accept a tosijs proxy as the value it wraps.** Additive for code that never meets
  tosijs; nothing else is unwrapped.

### Fixed since rc.6

- **A list parameter checks its elements against a named Type or an object shape** (#3403).
  `books: [Book]` was "array of any" and accepted `[5]`: a declared `Type` was resolved for a
  lone parameter and for union members, but not inside a list or an object member. And
  `[{ title: '', pages: 0 }]` checked only that each element was an object. Both are now
  checked element by element (members, nested shapes and nested lists), the same order of
  work as `[0.0]`, which was always checked. Code that passed malformed elements to such a
  parameter now gets an error value instead.
- **`Book | null` admits null again wherever a declared Type is promoted** (rc.7 review): as a
  parameter, a list item (`[Book | null]`) and an object member (`{ top: Book | null }`).
  Promotion replaced the type with a bare declared one and dropped the `| null`; the
  top-level case had done so since before rc.6.

### Added since rc.6

- **TJS works with tosijs models.** tosijs hands back proxies (`calculator.x` wraps a
  number). JavaScript uses them dynamically; TJS did not, which is exactly the friction it
  exists to remove: a typed `press(state: { x: 0 })` said "expected integer, got object" for a
  model whose `x` was a good number, `calculator.op == '+'` was false, and `if
  (calculator.op)` was true for an empty op. Now parameter checks, `Type.check` (and
  `Generic`/`Enum`/`Union`), `==`, truthiness, `given` and the test harness's `expect` all
  see the value a tosijs proxy wraps, while a function still RECEIVES the proxy, so writing to
  it updates the model and the page. Recognised by tosijs's `Symbol.for('xin-value')` (no
  dependency on tosijs); a `Date`, a `valueOf` object or a boxed primitive is checked as
  before. Checked with real tosijs proxies on the doc site.
  **Not yet:** a proxy held INSIDE a plain object or list (`{ a: calculator.x }`,
  `[calculator.x]`), an overloaded function's dispatch, and a `:?` return check still see the
  proxy and refuse it. Pass the model or the member directly, as the book does.

- **`tjs().testRunner` checks signature examples** (#3375). A return example
  (`greet(name: 'Ada'): 'Hello, Ada!'`) is a test the build runs, but the runner `tjs()`
  returns, which hosts such as tosijs-ui run for live examples, carried only `test` blocks, so
  a wrong example was never reported on a live page. It now carries them too, compared with
  the shared `expect().toEqual`. An example whose call throws is inconclusive (PRINCIPLES.md):
  it goes to a new `inconclusive` list in the runner's result, never to `results`, which hosts
  count. Async examples are not checked, as at build time. A differential test requires the
  page and the build to agree on every signature example in the docs.

### Documentation since rc.6

- **The TJS Programming Language, Part I, "Learn to Program", is complete** (chapters 0 to
  11): values and names, functions, checking your work (tests, taught right after
  functions), decisions, repetition, lists, things with parts, responding to the reader, a
  calculator (XY registers, a tested brain driving a tosijs model) and when things go wrong.
  Every example runs on tjs.tosijs.net and ends in tests the reader can see pass, and
  `doc-snippets.test.ts` runs them with stand-ins for the page.

## [0.14.0-rc.6] — 2026-10-17

On the `rc` dist-tag. One breaking change: `||` in a type is a compile error (a union is
spelled `|`). Plus a fix for annotations on nested functions, and documentation whose every
example now runs its tests. Pin `0.14.0-rc.6` exactly to test it.

### Read this first: what breaks since rc.5

- **`||` in a type is a compile error**, in TJS and AJS alike. `x: '' || null` never meant
  "string or null" (it rejected null); write `'' | null`. The error names the corrected
  spelling. A default (`x = a || b`) is still JavaScript, but its type is still read from the
  left side, so `x = '' || null` is a string parameter that defaults to null and then rejects
  it: write `x = '' | null` for a nullable string with a default.

### Changed since rc.5

- **BREAKING: `||` in a type is a compile error; a union is spelled `|`** (#3148).
  `x: '' || null` and `): T || null` were taught by three docs as "string or null" and never
  meant it: an example's `||` is JavaScript's OR, so the type was only the left side and
  `null` was REJECTED. Every type position (an annotation, an object member, an array
  element, a union member, a return annotation) now fails with the corrected spelling:
  `` `'' || null` reads as JavaScript OR … Write `'' | null` (one bar).`` This covers
  optional annotations (`x?:`) and AJS too, and the error points at the annotation's own
  line. A default (`x = a || b`) is still JavaScript (see "what breaks" above). The docs now
  use `|`, and a docs-tombstones row keeps it.

### Fixed since rc.5

- **An annotation on a function inside an expression is no longer a default value** (#3147).
  `items.map((x: 0) => x * 2)`, `a || ((x: '' | null) => x)`, `{ f: (x: 0) => x }` and
  every other arrow or function expression that is an operand, argument, array element,
  property or return value emitted `(x = 0) => …`: the example became a runtime default, so
  a missing argument was silently `0` (or, for `'' | null`, the number `0`). The annotation
  is now stripped, as it already was for declarations, named arrows, methods and class
  fields. These functions are not validated yet; that is a larger change.

### Documentation since rc.5

- **Every book snippet runs its own tests.** Twelve snippets across TJS-SYNTAX, TJS-FOR-JS,
  TJS-FOR-TS and the TJS guide wrote a return example as a type (`greet(name: 'World'): ''`,
  which TJS checks as a worked example: `greet('World')` must return `''`), or used the `||`
  union that never worked. Each now has a real worked result or `:!` (type only), and

- **TJS-FOR-JS described the return test wrongly.** It said TJS checks the result "is a
  number"; it checks the result equals the example (deep equality). It now says so, and

- **The TJS Programming Language opens with "Learn to Program"**, chapters 0 to 2 (How This

## [0.14.0-rc.5] — 2026-10-09

On the `rc` dist-tag. `==` and `!=` now group their operands as JavaScript does (the rewrite
is an AST pass), `tjs()` returns its runtime prelude separately for REPL hosts, and npm links
to the documentation site. Pin `0.14.0-rc.5` exactly to test it. This section is what changed
since rc.4; the notes for 0.14.0 as a whole, rc.1 to rc.4, are under the 0.14.0 heading
below.

### Read this first: what changes since rc.4

- **`==` and `!=` group their operands as JavaScript does.** Expressions the old rewrite
  grouped wrongly now compute what JavaScript would: `await f() == 3` compares the awaited
  value, `a & b == c` is `a & (b == c)`, and nested or chained `==` work. Code that relied
  on the old grouping gets a different, correct, answer. Everything else is additive.

### Added since rc.4

- **`tjs()` returns its runtime prelude separately**: `prelude` (the inline-runtime setup at
  the head of `code`, or `''`) and `body` (`code` without it). `code` is unchanged. A REPL
  host evaluating one line needs them apart: with the setup in front, a declaration evaluated
  to the setup's last assignment, and a line needing `await` had no value (tosijs-ui's
  console, #3134). Evaluate `prelude`, then `body`, in one scope.

### Fixed since rc.4

- **npm, the README and `llms.txt` name the documentation site** (tjs.tosijs.net) as the
  project's home. `package.json` had no `homepage`, so npm linked nowhere, and the README
  and `llms.txt` sent readers only to the older playground. A test keeps the three in
  agreement.
- **`==` and `!=` group their operands as JavaScript does.** The rewrite to `Eq`/`NotEq` was a
  text scanner that re-derived operator precedence by hand, and got it wrong in several
  shapes, all in released versions:
  - `await f() == 3` compared the Promise: `false` when `f()` resolved to 3. Reported by
    tosijs-ui's review of its dialect-aware console.
  - `(a == b) == (b == c)` emitted garbage that threw at run time, and `a == b == c` did not
    parse.
  - `a & b == c` (and `|`, `^`) grouped as `Eq(a & b, c)`; JavaScript reads `a & (b == c)`.
  - `void a == b` became `void Eq(a, b)`.

  The rewrite is now an AST pass in the emitter, beside the truthiness rewrite
  (`bool-coercion.ts`), so acorn decides the grouping. A differential test generates 928
  expressions across the precedence table and requires TJS to agree with JavaScript
  (`equality-precedence.test.ts`). Test and mock bodies that use `await` now get the
  truthiness rewrite too: their wrapper did not parse `await`, so such a body was skipped.

  Inside a `wasm {}` body, `==` and `!=` stay JavaScript's, which is what the compiled WASM
  does (`x != x` is the NaN test), so the body and its implicit JavaScript fallback agree. An
  explicit `fallback {}` is the author's own code and has TJS semantics, as before.

## [0.14.0] — unreleased

> **Release candidate: `0.14.0-rc.4`** (2026-10-07), on the `rc` dist-tag. WASM blocks mean
> what they say (a block that cannot compile is a compile error, and the WASM path and the
> fallback give the same answer), `predicate =>` is removed, and the deprecated `unsafe` prefix
> no longer escapes `var` or `eval`. Read "what breaks since rc.3" first. Pin `0.14.0-rc.4`
> exactly to test it.

### Read this first: what breaks since rc.3

Each of these breaks toward correctness; none has a compatibility switch.

- **A `wasm {}` block that cannot compile stops the transpile** (it used to ship its
  `fallback {}` with a warning). Fix the block, or drop the `wasm` wrapper. The error names
  the construct, the function and the line.
- **`%` and bitwise operators on f64 operands in WASM are refused**; `/` is now JavaScript's
  division even for two `i32` operands (`Math.trunc(a / b)` for integer division).
- **`predicate => expr` is a compile error**: write `predicate(x) { return expr }`.
- **`unsafe var` and `unsafe eval(…)` are refused**, as the docs already said: there is no
  escape for either. `unsafe` itself is deprecated; `LegacyDate(x)` replaces `unsafe new
  Date(x)`, and `new X(…)` on a class declared in the file needs no escape (drop `new`).
- **Emitted JavaScript has a different shape.** Test blocks, doc comments and the hashbang are
  blank lines in the output rather than removed, so line N of the output's body is line N of
  the source. Anything matching exact emitted text will see different line numbers.

### Changed since rc.3 — a `wasm {}` block means what its `fallback {}` means

Found by reviewing the WASM QuickStart, whose first example printed `undefined` (it promised
7). Each is pinned by `src/lang/wasm-semantics.test.ts`, which runs functions through WASM and
through the fallback and requires the same answer.

- **A statement that computes a value and throws it away is a compile error** that names the
  fix (`write \`return a + b\``). A block returns only with `return`, as in JavaScript; a bare
  final `a + b` compiled to a function with NO result. ASSUMPTIONS L6 decided this in 2026-08
  and it was never built. It found the same bug in `examples/wasm-demo.tjs` (three functions
  returning `undefined`) and in the prose of the `wasm-basics` example.
- **`/` is JavaScript's division** in a wasm block, even with two integer operands (`7 / 2` is
  `3.5`, not `3`). The old integer-division warning is retired: there is nothing left to warn
  about.
- **`let` is block-scoped**: two sibling `for (let i …)` loops compile, instead of colliding
  ("Duplicate local declaration") and silently running the fallback.
- **The WAT comment says `(result f64)` only when the function returns a value.**
- An unsafe (`!`) function no longer warns that a typed-array parameter "could not be resolved
  to a runtime type": it asked for no checks.
- **A `wasm` block that cannot compile is a compile error** (BREAKING for code that relied on
  the quiet fallback). `wasm { }` is a request for WASM; an unsupported construct used to ship
  the block's JavaScript `fallback {}` with a warning. The error names the construct. `fallback {}`
  remains for a RUNTIME that cannot run WASM. Turning this on found four test fixtures and a
  DOCS-TJS example that had never compiled (each passed by running its fallback), the DOCS-TJS
  page teaching a `wasm (…)` form that was never implemented, and the bugs below.
- **One bad block could take WASM away from a whole file.** `%` (or a bitwise operator) on f64
  operands emitted an `i32` instruction on f64 values; the module was invalid, so every block in
  the file ran its fallback while each reported success. It is now refused, naming the operator,
  and every emitted module is validated, so a future codegen bug of that kind is a compile error
  rather than a module that fails to load.
- **`f32x4_load`/`f32x4_store` need a typed-array parameter**, as `arr[i]` did: on a plain array
  they compiled and then threw a WebAssembly `RuntimeError` on the first call.
- **A file with WASM loads where WebAssembly is unavailable** (iOS Lockdown Mode): its memory
  was created unguarded at load, so a file whose blocks use typed arrays threw before any
  fallback could run. Its blocks now run their fallbacks and `wasmBuffer` hands out ordinary
  typed arrays.
- DOCS-WASM documents `i32` (in `wasm function` declarations) with its measured semantics:
  truncating and wrapping at the call, wrapping `+ - *`, a throwing `% 0`.

### Fixed since rc.3

- **Compile errors name the right line.** `extractTests` cut test blocks out, collapsed blank
  lines and trimmed, so every error below a `test` block or a few comment lines pointed at the
  wrong line (`src/lang/diagnostic-lines.test.ts`).
- The WASM QuickStart is rewritten: every example asserts its result and compiles to WASM
  (checked), and it states the supported subset and that anything else is a compile error.
  DOCS-WASM no longer lists `Math.sin`/`cos`/`log`/`exp`/`pow` as supported; a block using one
  does not compile.
- The TJS-vs-TypeScript page shows what each compiler actually did: what the program printed,
  or its compile error quoted verbatim (checked by `differences.test.ts`), instead of a
  one-row table where **rejected** sat where a printed value would go.
- Diagnostics no longer recommend the deprecated `unsafe` marker: `var` and `eval` have no
  escape, a raw `Date` is `LegacyDate(x)`, and `new P` simply says to drop the keyword. The
  docs no longer teach it either (a `docs-tombstones` row keeps it that way), and the
  CodeMirror integration no longer offers it as a completion; it offers `LegacyDate`.
- **`unsafe var` and `unsafe eval(…)` compiled** although every diagnostic said there was no
  escape: the checks ran on source with the `unsafe` spans masked. They now run on the raw
  source. `dialect: 'js'` still accepts both (TJS ⊇ JS).
- **`wasm` is TJS syntax only.** Under `dialect: 'js'`, `return wasm` followed by a block on
  the next line (legal JavaScript, by ASI) was rewritten and then refused.
- **The wasm compile error wins over a failing signature example**: the block is compiled
  before the transpile-time tests run, so `%` on f64 operands no longer reports "signature
  example is inconsistent… got undefined".
- **Each failing wasm block is reported at its own line**, and a `wasm function` by name. Two
  blocks sharing a first line both pointed at the first, and a repeated body pointed at the
  previous block's `fallback {}`.
- **`wasm function f(x: 0.0): 0.0` parses.** The return annotation accepted only an
  identifier (`: f64`), so the idiomatic numeric example was passed through as JavaScript and
  failed with "Unexpected token".
- A WASM module that is invalid with no single block responsible fails every block (a
  compile error) rather than being returned as success.
- **`stripModuleSyntax` parses** instead of using line regexes: a template literal with a line
  starting `export` survives, and top-level `await` and imports are handled. It now shares its
  implementation with `stripExports`.
- **Blanked regions cost lines, not bytes.** The padding that keeps offsets during the rewrite
  is dropped from the output (trailing whitespace only, never inside a string or template), so
  100 lines of doc comment no longer triple a module's size.

### Added since rc.3

- **`stripExports`** from `tjs-lang/lang` and `tjs-lang/browser` (#3109): turns a module into a

> object literal shaped like a VM node (`{ $expr: … }`) stays data too. A `while` body is now a
> block, so a `const` in it no longer fails on the second iteration (#2343). **Compatibility:**
> v1 ASTs — every stored procedure, everything the fluent builder writes (it still writes v1;
> its strings mean references) — keep v1 meaning, read by the same VM; an older VM refuses a v2
> AST by version, by name. Frozen by golden fixtures for both versions.
>
> **Since rc.1 — custom atoms receive VALUES.** An atom defined with `defineAtom` and written like
> the documented example (`async ({ url }) => fetch(url)`) received the variable's NAME when a
> program passed one — `echo({ v: local })` got `"local"` — in every earlier release. The VM now
> resolves inputs before calling it, and runs it under a context where `resolveValue` is the
> identity: an atom written the old way, calling `resolveValue` on its own inputs, keeps working
> and cannot re-evaluate guest data shaped like `{ $expr: … }` as code. Dynamic `cost` and
> `timeoutMs` functions see the same resolved input — so a cost function written against raw
> nodes (testing for `$expr`, or for a variable name) now receives values and must be updated.
> Steps an atom builds and runs itself — on the context it received, or on a scope from
> `createChildScope(ctx)` — run normally under either setting: the VM never runs a step under
> the resolved-inputs context. Running them on a COPY of that context, or after replacing its
> `state`, is refused by name rather than silently writing the caller's scope. **An atom that
> takes steps AS INPUT** must pass `{ resolveInputs: false }`, or its steps arrive evaluated
> as values.
>
> **Since rc.1 — the VM's budgets are invariants, not patches** ([`docs/vm-budgets.md`](docs/vm-budgets.md)).
> Five rc.2 review rounds in a row found one more place where guest code could allocate or hold
> memory that neither fuel nor `maxHeapBytes` saw — each fix closed one place and the next
> review found another. They are now three rules, each checked by a test that probes behaviour:
>
> - **Nothing allocates before it is charged.** Every operation whose allocation depends on
>   runtime data bounds it from its INPUTS and charges fuel and heap first. `'x'.repeat(5e8)`
>   built 1GB and then charged; `Array.from({ length: 3e8 })` charged nothing — any guest could
>   take the host's memory for under one unit of fuel, no capability needed.
> - **Every byte that outlives its step is charged where it lands** — a bind, an in-place
>   insertion (`push`, `fill`, a Set's `add`), a `memoize` store, a loop's results.
> - **Everything holding guest values while guest steps run is measured** — scopes, memo caches,
>   arguments, and the arrays a loop holds. Before a run fails, the VM measures the live heap
>   from those (each object once, every slot a pointer) plus the in-flight allocations of the
>   steps still running, and fails only if THAT is over; the error reports it.
>
> **The guest method allowlist is now a table,** and a method without a declared allocation
> bound is not callable. Gone (breaking, though none of them could be used well): the legacy
> HTML string methods (`bold`, `link`, …), callback methods that guest code has no functions to
> pass to (`forEach`, `every`, `flatMap`, … — use `for…of` or `map`/`filter`/`find`/`reduce`),
> `matchAll` and the array `keys`/`values`/`entries` (they returned host iterators), the
> `__lookupGetter__` family (it returned a host function), and `toString` on a builtin function —
> `Date.toString()` returned the host's SOURCE CODE. A long string held under several names
> still counts once per name (fails closed). With everything since rc.1 below, the VM grew ~30%:
> `tjs-lang/vm-ast` is 37 KB gzipped, `tjs-lang/vm` 88 KB (68 KB at rc.1); the regex engine is
> about 7 KB of it, the closed schema dialect and data-only `Schema` about 2 KB.
>
> **Since rc.1 — `$predicate` runs only source the host trusts (breaking).** A predicate compiles
> to native JavaScript, and a syntactic verifier cannot make hostile JavaScript safe: one review
> round found five more routes from a "verified" predicate to the host's regex engine
> (`['(a+)+$',''].reduce(RegExp)`, a method passed as a callback, a tagged template, a class
> shadowing a name, overwriting a field). So the `$predicate` paths — `createPredicateEvaluator`
> (what `tjs-lang/schema` installs), `compilePredicateSchema`, `validatePredicateSchema` — run a
> source only if the host registered it with `trustPredicate(source)` (`tjs-lang/css`'s schema
> builders register theirs), or passed `trustAllPredicates: true`. Anything else fails closed,
> saying why. **Migration:** wrap your own `$predicate` sources in `trustPredicate(…)`; never
> trust a source that arrived as data. Running untrusted predicates on the AJS VM, whose surface
> is a closed table, is planned and will lift this. A source trusted after a first refusal runs at
> once (the evaluator checks trust on every call); its cache is bounded. In predicates, a
> string-literal pattern (`s.search('@')`) runs on the metered engine rather than being refused.
>

> items (`s.size` is its length, by every route; `Array.isArray(s)` is true), and a `Date` is a
> frozen object of its fields — `value` (ISO), `timestamp`, `year`, `month` (1–12), `day`,
> `hours`, `minutes`, `seconds`, `dayOfWeek` — all in UTC, so a program's output does not depend
> on the host's time zone (fields, `add` and `format` used local time). A Date has ONE form:
> guest `JSON.stringify`, a capability's input and the run result all see the object, where rc.1
> wrote the ISO string — write `d.value` for that. `Date(x)` takes every form a date takes: a
> guest Date, a stored one (an object with a numeric `timestamp`, which is what a Date becomes
> after JSON, a store or a capability), a number of ms within the Date range, or a string that
> parses; `Date.parse` is the same door. `format`'s keywords (`'ISO'`, `'date'`, `'time'`) are
> case-insensitive. A regex is an object of its `source` and flags. Their methods are the VM's, dispatched by kind, so a value never carries a
> function: the sealed wrappers and the run-result conversion that kept their methods away from
> guest code are gone, with the four defects the seventeenth re-review found in them (a recursive
> conversion that a deep or self-containing Set crashed, a `__proto__` key, an uncharged walk of
> an `Object.assign` target, conversion only at the result). `push` and `Object.assign` into a Set
> are refused (use its methods), and reading a method as a value (`const f = s.add`) is refused as
> it is on a string. An in-place insertion is now checked and charged BEFORE it happens, so a
> refused value is never left behind for a `catch` to reach. `agentRun` hands a sub-agent exactly
> what it was passed: it resolved the input twice (a string that named a caller variable became
> that variable's value) and evaluated an inline sub-agent's expressions in the CALLER's scope.
> Sub-agent and `runCode` arguments are null-prototype, like `vm.run`'s. `pick` again copies any
> own data property (`pick(arr, ['length'])`), never a function. An AST's `inputSchema` is
> validated before the run's timer exists, so it is now capped on the product — 1M argument paths
> and 1e8 schema-node × path steps (about 0.6s) — and refused past either: validate in the host,
> or pass smaller arguments. A guest-program fuzzer (`src/vm/guest-fuzz.test.ts`) now checks the
> invariants over random programs.

> **Since rc.1 — `httpFetch` follows no redirects and admits only known headers; the VM never
> writes to your capabilities (security, breaking).** In allowlist mode `httpFetch` compared only
> the hostname, so on Bun or Deno `file://<allowed-host>/etc/hosts` read a host file. Every request
> is now admitted by one rule: the scheme must be `http:` or `https:` in both modes, then the
> allowlist, and without an allowlist nothing is fetched.
> - **No redirects are followed.** A redirect (301, 302, 303, 307 or 308 with a `Location`) comes
>   back to the agent as data, `{ redirect: true, status, location }`, with `location` resolved to
>   an absolute URL, and fetching it is a new request, admitted like any other with its headers
>   and body chosen afresh. A 304 Not Modified, or any other 3xx, is an ordinary response. In a
>   browser `location` is null, because the browser hides it. Four review rounds each found another redirect rule the VM had
>   re-implemented wrong (credentials re-sent, then the body re-sent on 307/308, then on 301/302
>   for PUT, PATCH and DELETE), so the built-in client stopped following redirects. A host that
>   wants them followed supplies a `fetch` capability.
> - **Guest request headers are a closed list:** `Accept`, `Accept-Language`, `Authorization`,
>   `Cache-Control`, `Content-Language`, `Content-Type`, the `If-*` validators, `Range`,
>   `User-Agent`, `X-API-Key`, `X-Request-Id`, `X-Correlation-Id` and `X-Requested-With`. A host
>   adds names for a run with `context.allowedRequestHeaders`, as it does with
>   `allowedFetchDomains`. Anything else is refused by name, never dropped, and `X-Agent-Depth` is
>   refused even if a host lists it. A guest `Host` was sent as given, and on Bun behind a
>   Host-routing proxy it reached virtual hosts outside the allowlist. A denylist kept growing, and
>   so did an "X- except the routing ones" rule (`X-Envoy-Original-Dst-Host`, `X-Originating-IP`, …),
>   so neither survived.
> - **A host's own `fetch` capability** receives the agent's request after the same admission.
>   The request's SHAPE is admitted on every path, always: `http:`/`https:` only (`file://` read
>   a host file through the documented `safeFetch` on Bun), the method and the headers. Its
>   DESTINATION (`allowedFetchDomains`, with ports) is enforced on every path when set; without
>   it, a host fetch owns the destination. Redirects and `credentials` are then the host's; the
>   documented `safeFetch` refuses redirects and omits credentials.
> - **`Eval` and `SafeFunction` take a host-only `fetchPolicy`** (`{ domains, methods, headers }`),
>   forwarded to the run and never visible to guest code. Their `context` option is guest
>   variables, so before this they could not allow a POST at all.
> - **Migration, hosts with their own `fetch`:** an agent's POST, PUT or DELETE now needs
>   `context.allowedFetchMethods` (or `fetchPolicy.methods`), and headers outside the closed list
>   need `context.allowedRequestHeaders` (or `fetchPolicy.headers`).
> - **The built-in `httpFetch` is a demonstration capability, highly constrained by default**
>   (Tonio). A real deployment supplies its own `fetch`. **Methods:** GET and HEAD by default;
>   a host enables more for a run with `context.allowedFetchMethods`. CONNECT, TRACE and TRACK
>   are never admitted. **Ports:** an `allowedFetchDomains` entry admits the scheme's default port
>   only, unless it names one (`api.example.com:8443`); matching the hostname alone admitted
>   every port of an allowed host. **One admission, every path:** the agent's method and headers
>   are admitted the same way when a host's own `fetch` sends the request, so a host that needs
>   `Cookie` or PROPFIND declares it.
> - **No browser credentials:** cookies and HTTP auth are not sent (`credentials: 'omit'`); a
>   custom `fetch` can opt in.
> - **Bounded body:** the body is read under `membraneMaxBytes` (a larger declared
>   `Content-Length` is refused before reading) and aborted once the cap is exceeded, not
>   buffered whole first.
>
> Separately, `vm.run` used to write its default in-memory store INTO the capabilities object you
> passed, so two runs sharing that object shared the store, and a frozen object made the run throw.
> The VM now uses your capabilities object exactly as passed: it is never copied, wrapped or
> written, so a class instance with private fields or getters works as it always did.
> - The default store belongs to the run and is used only when your object has no `store`.
> - **Custom atoms:** read the store through `storeOf(ctx)`, not `ctx.capabilities.store`, which
>   is now the host's own object and undefined when the host gave none.
> - Each run, nested runs included, has its own default store.
> - A non-object `capabilities` is refused.
>
> In AJS, an atom input named `op`, `result`, `resultConst` or `resultAssign` is refused at
> transpile time: it was silently read as a step control field.
>
> Image URLs follow the same rule as a fetch, in `llmVision` and in `llmPredictBattery` message
> arrays: the model server may fetch an http(s) `image_url` itself. Inline base64 image data passes
> (`data:image/…` or `data:application/octet-stream`, parameters allowed, which is what
> `httpFetch`'s `dataUrl` returns). http(s) passes only against the run's `allowedFetchDomains`,
> and is refused without one. What reaches the model server is the ADMITTED, normalised URL: a
> backslash-userinfo URL that one parser reads as an allowed host and another as `169.254.169.254`
> is never forwarded as written. `llmPredictBattery` takes a string or a message array, which the
> VM REBUILDS from a closed shape (`{ role, content }`, content a string or `text`/`image_url`
> parts; any other part type, such as `video_url`, is refused) and forwards with the admitted image
> URLs; the shipped battery sends it as the conversation itself. The `{ text, images }` vision form
> is refused there (use `llmVision`). With an allowlist set, a fetch URL that is not absolute is
> refused, because it names no host to check. A NETWORK-PATH reference (`//host/x` and its
> backslash forms) is refused on every path, since it borrows the page's scheme. A host's `fetch`
> always receives the ADMITTED, normalised URL, never the raw input. A policy list that is not an
> array of strings is refused (a string was read one character at a time). Rebinding a value already in scope (a
> per-iteration `let p = o`) costs one pointer again: in rc.2's heap accounting it re-measured
> the whole value, so a loop was quadratic in fuel where rc.1 was linear.

> **Since rc.1 — an outbound membrane on capability calls (security, breaking for some custom
> atoms).** What an IO atom hands a capability is now a budgeted deep COPY of its resolved input,
> checked against the input schema the atom declares (Tonio). The inbound membrane already did this
> for what a capability returns. The outbound direction kept being found one site at a time:
> - a `system` or `prompt` that was really an array of `video_url` parts;
> - `tools` and `responseFormat` forwarded live, so a guest that caught a timeout changed them
>   before a slow host serialised them;
> - raw URLs.
>
> It applies to every core, battery and custom IO atom whose inputs the VM resolves, and fails by
> refusing (`'<op>': its input does not have the shape the atom declares`). **Embedders:** a custom
> IO atom now receives plain-data copies, and is called only with inputs matching its declared
> schema; a `storeGet` key must be the string it declares. An IO atom with
> `resolveInputs: false` should pass what it hands a capability through the newly exported
> `egressValue`. `agentRun`'s capability route and `cache` now do (both handed the host live guest
> objects), and a `cache` key must be a string.
>
> The copy is paid for. Its walk is budgeted by the run's remaining fuel and by
> `membraneMaxBytes`, which **now caps both directions** (it was documented for returns only).
> The copy is charged as an allocation before it is made, and a call that is refused is charged
> for the walk it caused. The first version of this membrane charged nothing, so a loop over a
> large value used about 100× the CPU for the same fuel (cumulative review 5).
>
> **`cache` and `memoize` require a key (breaking).** A key-less block derived its key by calling
> the `hash` atom's step wrapper, which returns nothing, so every key-less block was stored under
> `undefined` and returned ANOTHER block's result; a `cache` entry is shared across runs for 24
> hours by default. Keying by a digest of the steps is no better: the steps are the same when the
> data they read is not. Only the author knows what a result depends on, so the builder's `key`
> is now required and the VM refuses a block without one. A store written by an earlier version
> may hold a stale `cache:undefined` entry; it is safe to delete. A key larger than
> `membraneMaxBytes` is refused like any other capability input, and a result too large to cross
> fails the step rather than being returned uncached.
>
> **IO atoms declare their inputs (breaking for embedders).** `defineAtom` refuses an IO atom
> (`effects: 'io'`, the default) with no input schema (use `s.object({})` for none), or whose input
> schema contains `pattern`/`patternProperties`: the outbound membrane validates every call
> against that schema, so a pattern there ran on the host's regex engine over guest-chosen
> strings, outside fuel. Check patterns in the atom's body. (The JSON Schema direction is Pattern:
> `docs/pattern.md`.) The schema is admitted as a frozen plain-JSON COPY when the atom is
> defined, and every call is validated against that copy: a `pattern` is refused whatever its
> value (a RegExp included), any other non-JSON value is refused rather than converted, and
> changing `atom.inputSchema` afterwards changes nothing. An atom tagged `io` after definition is
> admitted at its first call. Migration:
>
> ```js
> defineAtom('ping', undefined, s.any, fn)               // refused
> defineAtom('ping', s.object({}), s.any, fn)            // takes nothing
> defineAtom('lookup', s.object({ id: s.string.pattern('^[a-z]+$') }), …) // refused:
> defineAtom('lookup', s.object({ id: s.string }), …)    // check the id in the body
> ```
>
> A refused outbound copy is billed for the work its walk did, whatever refused it, never more
> than the fuel present, and keeps its own error unless fuel genuinely ran out. Round 31 billed
> only a refusal for size (a depth refusal after a megabyte was free); round 32 billed the whole
> budget on top of what the copy had already been charged (cumulative reviews 6 and 7).
>
> **A refusal at the capability boundary that is a bug ends the run (breaking).** An atom call
> whose input does not match the atom's declared schema, a value refused on its way out to a
> capability (too large, too deep, not plain data, over the heap ceiling or the fuel), and a
> capability's RETURN that JSON could not express (a function, a getter, a class instance: the
> host's contract broken) can no longer be caught
> by `try`/`catch`. A return that is merely too large or too deep (things JSON can do), or does not
> match the atom's declared output, is the world's doing and stays catchable (Tonio), and every inbound copy is billed in fuel so a
> retry loop pays. A value an atom THROWS reaches a guest `catch` as a capped string: its
> `message` (read once, so a `DOMException`'s works), or `String(value)` for a thrown primitive;
> never an object (a thrown `{ message: obj }` used to hand over a live host object). A typed
> array over a `SharedArrayBuffer`, or any subclass of a typed array, `DataView` or `Date`, is
> refused at the boundary: `structuredClone` would SHARE that memory with the guest, not copy it. Refusals that end the run: no catch block, later step or parent-agent step runs, and the
> run reports the refusal. This includes a `cache` entry or key that cannot cross, and persisted
> ASTs or builder programs that wrapped such a call in `try`. Ordinary failures (a fetch that fails, a store that throws) are caught as before. Four
> review rounds in a row (cumulative reviews 5 to 8) each found a refusal path billed short of the
> work it did, and each mattered only because a guest could catch the refusal and retry it in a
> loop. A refusal that ends the run costs at most one bounded walk (Tonio).
>
> **The membrane builds its copy: JSON plus Date (breaking).** Every value crossing the capability
> boundary (capability returns, IO-atom inputs, run arguments) is now a copy the membrane builds
> from exactly what it read, instead of a `structuredClone` of the original. `structuredClone`
> copies internal slots the check never saw, so a typed array over a `SharedArrayBuffer` with a
> shadowed `buffer`, a prototype-swapped buffer, or a 1-byte view over 50MB was checked as one
> thing and forwarded as another (cumulative review 13). What crosses is plain objects, arrays,
> strings, numbers, booleans, null/undefined, and `Date` (by its internal time). **`Map`, `Set`,
> typed arrays, `ArrayBuffer`, `RegExp` and `Error` no longer cross**: a capability returning one,
> or a run argument containing one, is refused. Convert them to JSON first (a Map to an object or
> an array of pairs). Shared references and cycles are preserved, as before. A `Date` crosses only
> when it is exactly an intrinsic `Date` (a subclass, or one with own fields, would arrive thinned).
> Cost, measured: a 300-document RAG return copies in ~1.9ms (3.5ms before); a 400k-number array
> in ~143ms (~127ms before), where the per-element descriptor read that keeps getters from
> running dominates, as it did.

> null prototype and given their real one when complete, so a polluted `Object.prototype` setter
> never runs on capability data and frozen intrinsics (SES) do not refuse ordinary JSON. A
> crossing is bounded by `membraneMaxBytes` and (outbound) the remaining fuel; the heap ceiling
> applies where the value lands. A refusal for size names the limit that set it. Fixed in the
> same rounds: rc.2 builds briefly read `SharedArrayBuffer` at module scope, which threw on
